before: News of the Southern succession has reached Dongzhou. The Zheng maritime empire that we fought for independence is again divided over who should rule it. Its opponents may seek support from our republic, while merchants watch for changes to the ports and routes on which they depend.\n\nWe can pursue those openings, but assistance abroad will draw on our own treasury and industry. The government must decide which relationships serve the republic and which commitments it can sustain.
after: News of the Southern succession has reached Dongzhou. The Zheng maritime empire we once fought for our independence is now split over who should rule it. Zheng's enemies may come to the republic for help, and the merchants are watching what becomes of the ports and sea lanes.\n\nIt is a chance to widen our ties abroad. But every subsidy we send abroad comes out of the republic's own treasury and factories.

before: Southern envoys seek recognition and the continuation of old agreements, while India remains divided by disputes over the southern coast. French merchants, creditors and officers have interests in both regions. The government must decide whom to support and how far its money and arms should follow its diplomacy.
after: Southern envoys ask France to recognise the new dynasty and honour the old treaties. In India, the quarrel over the southern coast and the colonies is still unsettled. French merchants, creditors and officers have money riding on both.

before: Caravans from Sichuan have brought news of the Southern dispute. Since the defeat at Dunhuang, Western Qin has had to consider its military strength and finances carefully. Renewed war in the east would make the roads through Bashu more important to trade and security alike. We should decide whether to cultivate Sichuan, support the anti-Wu coalition, or keep our resources at home.
after: Caravans from Sichuan have brought news of the Southern dispute. After the defeat at Dunhuang, Western Qin cannot afford to squander men or money again. If war returns to the east, the Bashu roads will strain under trade and frontier defence at once.

before: News of the Southern succession has reached the northern republic. Exiles recognise familiar names among those now disputing power, and some are already seeking contacts in Dongzhou. A friendly republic might supply funds or arms, but our government must decide what help it needs and what relationship it can sustain.
after: News of the Southern succession has reached the northern republic. Exiles have spotted old names in the war reports, and some are already writing to comrades in Dongzhou. Old friendships like these might yet buy the republic money and guns.

before: The Southern succession may alter the court’s dealings with a powerful neighbour. Trade along the rivers and the obligations inherited from existing treaties remain immediate concerns. Before committing money or arms to either side, we must consider our own status and which government can best protect our interests.
after: The Southern succession will change how the court deals with its powerful neighbour. Neither the river trade nor the duties of the old treaties can be set aside. Before promising money or arms to anyone, the court must work out who can be trusted.

before: The Southern succession offers another opening to raise our claims on the Indian coast. Ming possessions in Mysore and the arrangements of coastal traders remain sources of contention. Our ministers may seek French assistance in money or arms. If Southern rule still holds land in Mysore, we can also press our territorial claim.
after: The Southern succession has reopened old accounts on the Indian coast. Ming holdings in Mysore and their coastal trading rights have long been a thorn in the empire's side. Our ministers can ask France for money and arms, and if the Southern court still holds land in Mysore, now is the moment to press our claim.

before: The old alliance between France and Ming placed heavy pressure on British trade routes. A disputed succession in the Southern realm may create openings for commerce and diplomacy. Merchants seek access to its ports, while the government weighs the expense of supporting a foreign partner.
after: While France and Ming stood together, British shipping was hemmed in on every route. Now the Southern succession is contested: merchants hope to slip into new ports, and London is free to choose its friends again.

before: Russia’s long eastern frontier gives the Southern dispute consequences far beyond its place of origin. A reliable trading partner or a government willing to accept our support might strengthen our position. We may wait for the outcome, or commit funds and arms while the rivals still need foreign friends.
after: Russia's eastern frontier is long, and the Southern dispute touches St Petersburg's interests too. A dependable trading partner, or a government willing to take our aid, would make Russia's position in the east easier. We can wait until the victor is clear, or spend money and arms now, while every side is still looking for friends.

before: The Southern succession has placed old treaties, trade routes and overseas dependencies in question. Our government must choose which relationships to cultivate and whether to offer assistance or seek it from abroad. Existing agreements continue to bind their parties while new proposals are negotiated.
after: The Southern succession has thrown old treaties, trade routes and the fate of overseas dependencies into doubt. Envoys are on the move: some come asking for help, others wait for us to speak first. Treaties already signed still bind those who signed them.

before: Attend to our own affairs first.
after: Our own house comes first.

after: [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_external_requester').GetName] has sent an envoy to request #v 10#! small arms under a treaty binding for #v 1 year#!. The bill of lading is already on the foreign ministry's desk.

before: Close the diplomatic mission and withdraw pending requests. Treaties already in force must be handled separately through diplomacy.
after: Fold up the letters of credence and withdraw any requests still awaiting an answer. Treaties already in force must be handled separately through diplomacy.

before: Resume negotiations while the Southern crisis remains unresolved. An aid agreement already concluded cannot be repeated through this mission.

before: The Southern succession has reached a settlement. Our envoys have completed their mission, but treaties already signed remain in force. The government must continue meeting those obligations and attend to the relationships that survive the crisis.
after: The Southern succession has been decided, and our envoys have come home to report. The treaties we signed still stand. Every payment and every shipment of arms they promise must still be delivered.

before: Our envoy has returned home. There is no longer a government to receive the letter concerning the Southern succession. Any treaties already signed remain in force.
after: There is no one left to receive our letters, and the envoy has come home. Treaties already signed will still be honoured.

before: Wu shipping brings grain from the Southern Seas, distant timber and foreign goods into the Southern realm. Inland workshops, garrisons and academies already depend on those exchanges. Provincial powers differ, but production and livelihoods can scarcely stand apart from the common market. Closing a port or severing a trade route spreads losses far beyond it.\n\nAs the Ming court and Hangzhou dispute the succession, [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] must keep its government and forces functioning. Offices need paper, garrisons need recruits and arms, and academy students are preparing to enter political life. We must maintain trade with willing partners and make local workshops, schools and livelihoods capable of enduring the present disruption.
after: Wu shipping brings grain from the Southern Seas, distant timber and foreign goods into the Southern realm. Inland workshops, garrisons and academies already depend on those exchanges. Provincial powers differ, but production and livelihoods can scarcely stand apart from the common market. Closing a port or severing a trade route spreads losses far beyond it.\n\nWhile the Ming court and Hangzhou fight over the succession, [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] cannot let its government or army stand still for a single day. They hope to maintain procurement contacts between the two countries and exchange information about supplies of paper, timber and manufactured goods, preserving trading opportunities as the political situation changes.\n\nThese contacts would broaden our commercial relations, but need officials to receive the mission and merchants to sustain the exchanges. [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] may appoint representatives to hear the proposed arrangements.
after: Envoys from [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_supply_requester').GetName] have brought a request from their merchants: keep a purchasing line open between our countries, share news of paper, timber and workshop supplies, so that merchants can still find a way to trade however the situation turns.\n\nSending someone to talk means officials to receive them and merchants to do the business. [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] could at least hear what they want to buy.

before: Our domestic affairs must come first.
after: We cannot even keep our own house in order. The merchants will have to wait.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_supply_requester').GetName] proposes a formal treaty granting reciprocal trade advantages. Merchants hope to expand their markets, while those buying supplies seek more stable commercial relations. Once signed, both countries will be obliged to fulfil its terms.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_supply_requester').GetName] proposes a formal treaty granting reciprocal trade advantages. Merchants hope it will open new markets, and buyers want steadier trading relations.

before: Immigrants and merchant ships built the republic’s coastal towns. War against Wu brought its states together; the northern alliance opened further markets. Work in the harbours, production in the mills and provincial revenue now depend upon these connections.\n\nNews of the southern dispute crosses the ocean. Whether we continue in the shared market or arrange our own trade, production and livelihoods at home must endure.
after: Immigrants and merchant ships built the republic's coastal towns. War against Wu brought its states together; the northern alliance opened further markets. Work in the harbours, production in the mills and provincial revenue now depend upon these connections.\n\nNow news of the Southern succession has crossed the ocean. Merchants ask after their supplies, shipowners fret about the sea lanes, and the workers are still waiting for their weekly wages. Whether we stay in the common market or go our own way, the first thing is to keep our own production, and our own livelihoods, steady.

before: Dye shipments connect the southern plantations to the imperial market. Rent, advances and debt bind many village households to that trade. New paid work and viable smallholdings will determine whether the interior can sustain its own customers and savings.
after: Dye shipments connect the southern plantations to the imperial market. Rent, advances and debt bind many village households to that trade. Tenasserim needs people to fell timber, haul cargo and run the port, and it needs rice fields that can still feed a family. Only when new hands are paid their wages and tenants keep their harvest will the interior have trade and savings of its own.

before: The Tenasserim programme has run into difficulty. Logging camps and workshops need employers able to pay wages. Villagers need tenancy and credit arrangements that leave them a livelihood. The practical instruction provided by the authorities also requires sustained funding.\n\nThe government must decide whether to keep committing resources or return these responsibilities to the existing administration and merchants.
after: Tenasserim's programme has hit trouble. The logging camps and workshops need employers willing to pay wages; villagers can keep their harvest only once tenancy and debt are sorted out; and the instructors sent by the authorities must be paid for year after year.

before: Land commissioners in [SCOPE.sState('cne_land_reform_mess_imprisonment_state').GetName] have arrested villagers who drafted petitions over disputed titles and placed them in military custody for concealing property. Officers widened the arrests to local gentry, teachers and clerks who kept the old deeds.\n\nThe new law empowers officials to settle land ownership, but also permits farmers to defend their property. The prisoners' families have taken their deeds to the provincial capital, and the governor has referred the case to the Ministry of Justice. The commissioners warn of collusion and unrest and ask the Ministry of War to protect the officers involved. Transferring a few officials would allow the affair to pass quietly. A prosecution would make the reform's own agents answer for crimes committed in its name.
after: Land commissioners in [SCOPE.sState('cne_land_reform_mess_imprisonment_state').GetName] have arrested villagers who drafted petitions over disputed titles and placed them in military custody for concealing property. Officers widened the arrests to local gentry, teachers and clerks who kept the old deeds.\n\nThe new law empowers officials to settle land ownership, but also permits farmers to defend their property. The prisoners' families have taken their deeds to the provincial capital, and the governor has referred the case to the Ministry of Justice. The commissioners, warning of collusion between soldiers and villagers and of possible unrest, have asked the Ministry of War to protect the officers involved.

before: The streets of [SCOPE.sState('cne_land_reform_peasants_in_city_state').GetName] are filling with newcomers from the countryside. Farming families have sold their land and come in search of wages. Employment brokers send them to factories and building sites, deducting recruitment and lodging charges from their pay.\n\nWorkers have accused the brokers of withholding contracts and enforcing old debts. Manufacturers fear that an inquiry will disrupt recruitment, while local gentry defend brokers linked to their own associations. The governor must decide whether to prosecute the organisations that bind workers to them or leave the disputes to ordinary civil proceedings. In these growing towns, the promise that peasants could leave their old estates and freely earn a living faces its first practical tests.
after: The streets of [SCOPE.sState('cne_land_reform_peasants_in_city_state').GetName] are filling with newcomers from the countryside. Farming families have sold their land and come in search of wages. Employment brokers send them to factories and building sites, deducting recruitment and lodging charges from their pay.\n\nWorkers have accused the brokers of withholding contracts and enforcing old debts. Manufacturers fear that an inquiry will hamper recruitment, while local gentry speak up for brokers linked to their own associations. The peasants have left the old estates behind, yet in town someone else still holds their contracts.

before: We must unite the Polish people, that's the justice not just for one nation but for all. We must also lay claim to our rightful lands.
after: We must unite the Polish people, that's the justice not just for one nation but for all.

before: We must prepare our military for the conflict ahead if we are to secure our independence.
after: We must prepare our military for the inevitable conflict.

before: Chen Dongyang is dead. Southern republicans have lost the leader of their reforms, while the cabinet and Six Ministries must redistribute his responsibilities. Provincial delegates still debate reform’s future in the Assembly of Rites, but Hangzhou is already courting the officials left without their leader.
after: Chen Dongyang, courtesy name Manyue, was the leading voice of citizen republicanism in the Western Qin Revolution and one of the founders of its short-lived republic. Driven out of the state he had helped create, he joined the southern progressives and, as chief minister of Southern Ming, became the leader of its modernising reforms.\n\nNow he is dead. The southern republicans who followed him have lost their mainstay, and the cabinet and Six Ministries must parcel out the duties he left behind. The provincial delegates are still arguing over the future of reform in the Assembly of Rites, but Hangzhou is already courting the leaderless officials.

before: The Zheng foothold in Kyushu forms part of Wu’s maritime power and has long affected the interests of Japan’s great houses. With civil war threatening the Southern realm, rival envoys cross the sea seeking ships and supplies. The government has an opportunity to recover the Wu-held lands of Kyushu and reshape relations across the strait.
after: The Toyotomi shogunate once ended the Warring States with the backing of the Ming Prince of Wu, and in the struggle for Korea joined him to defeat a Korea backed by the Ming court at Yanjing and the old Qi fief. From then on, the Zheng foothold in Kyushu became one link in Wu's maritime empire.\n\nNow the South is at war with itself, and envoys keep crossing the sea, asking Japan for ships and supplies. The chance to recover the Wu-held lands of Kyushu is right in front of us.

before: The Zheng family has demanded a new dynasty and recognition from the provinces and overseas states. Hangzhou’s military and fiscal power gives force to its claim, but the centuries-old Zhu succession still commands loyalty. The dispute unresolved in the Assembly of Rites and cabinet has now reached the provinces.\n\n[ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] must answer. Recognition accepts Zheng government under the new constitution. Taking up arms for Ming requires allies and preparations against Hangzhou’s forces. Others would use the crisis to leave the existing hierarchy and govern independently.
after: In the great hall at Jinling, no one is left who can stand up to the Zheng sovereign of Wu face to face. By the measure of China's thousands of years of history, a change of dynasty was only a matter of time. Yet those who cling to the old and those who chase the new alike believed our age had risen above history. Dreams seldom survive contact with reality.\n\nThe Zheng have now called for a new dynasty and demanded that the provinces and overseas states adopt the Wu calendar. Hangzhou holds the army and the purse, but the Zhu line, centuries old, still has its loyal followers. The quarrel that the Assembly of Rites and the cabinet could never settle has at last reached the provinces. [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] must give its answer.

before: Uphold Ming and rally the provinces!
after: Wu bandits! Curs! Traitors! Villains! Usurpers!

before: Let our government rule independently.
after: The sage does not stand beneath a collapsing wall. How can good men dwell in a traitor's land?

before: Petition for accession and recognise Wu.
after: How does the new regime's black hat feel?

before: Proclamations against the succession have spread. Wu is assembling the central army to enforce recognition of Zheng rule. Ming loyalist provinces are gathering troops and supplies for common resistance. The Southern and Western Administrations, once united against the North, now face one another in arms.\n\nMaritime and river trade routes will carry armies and suffer the disruption of war. Overseas dependencies, neighbouring states and distant merchants must choose their course anew. Whoever wins will inherit the demands of those who shed blood for victory.
after: Manifestos against the usurpation have spread to every province. Wu is mustering the central army to make the provinces accept Zheng rule; the Ming loyalist provinces are rallying their garrisons and scraping together men and grain for a common fight. The Southern and Western Administrations, who once stood shoulder to shoulder against the North, have come to blows after all.\n\nFrom the Far East Continent to distant England, the powers have sent envoys to ask what is happening. They will watch the East burst into flames once more after only a brief peace.

before: Raise funds and troops to uphold the new dynasty.
after: Send word to every camp: muster the men and the money at once!

before: Uphold Ming and unite against Wu.
after: By Heaven's mandate, end the nation's calamity! Slay the usurpers, restore the true calendar!

before: Unite against Wu, then establish government by the people.
after: Better to die for the broad light of our state than live serving partitionist kings! Long live the citizens! Long live the republic!

before: Honour our commitments in the mainland struggle.
after: When a minister coerces his lord from below, the Warring States age begins anew. Even Zheng pride has withered at last.

before: Watch the fighting and honour our commitments.
after: A shocking development.

before: Accession Without a General War
after: A Silent Dynastic Transfer

before: Local opposition has failed to form a coalition for common war. Provinces and overseas states that remain loyal recognise Zheng rule, while others have left the previous hierarchy. Hangzhou can continue governing the centre, but cannot treat every silence as consent.\n\nThe new dynasty must appoint officials and govern under its constitution, while sustaining authority with the troops and revenues it possesses. Unresolved relations with the provinces and states will be shaped by future development, negotiation and conflict.
after:
Rather than let the conflict explode, the South's statesmen used a string of decisive measures to put off the empire's collapse. Even through an upheaval as great as the passing of Ming to Wu, the provinces and overseas states that stayed loyal never took up arms, and swallowed the Wu account of a Ming court rotten to the core; a few others simply left the old hierarchy.

In a sense, the dynasty of sun and moon may long since have become a rotten trunk that no one would follow into the grave.

Yet this survivor, which crawled out of long centuries of military fiefdoms, has also lost a great deal. Opponents, regional prejudice between the peoples of the old fiefs, and new radical societies still move in the shadows of the new age, laying a thick fog over the country's road ahead.

before: Begin governing the new dynasty.
after: I too once wished to live in the age of Ming.

before: Authority After Victory
after: Victory in the Second Jingnan War

before: The coalition has defeated Wu’s central army. The Ming cause brought the Western provinces and their allies together; victory now raises another question: who will govern from Nanjing?\n\nThe Zhu house still claims the throne, while victorious provincial leaders are reluctant to surrender their military and political authority. Republicans want the citizens who fought together to share in a new deliberative government. Whether the wartime coalition can accommodate these demands will determine the Southern realm’s future constitution.
after: The civil war unleashed by the treacherous Zheng has ended at last in victory for us, the upholders of the rightful way. It was not an age to be proud of. Loyal servants slaughtered loyal servants, and republicans denounced republicans.\n\nOnly now that the war is won do the real difficulties come to the table. The Zhu house wants its throne back, the victorious provincial leaders will not give up their military and civil power, and the republicans want the citizens who fought side by side brought into a new deliberative government. Who, then, is to rule from Nanjing?

before: Restore the Zhu house to government.
after: Set chaos right and renew sun and moon under a new sky!

before: Retain Ming’s name under our government.
after: Wu's crime lies in disorderly governance, not central authority itself.

before: Let the people govern without another emperor.
after: We couldn't win it in 1812. We'll try again today!

before: Representatives of [SCOPE.sCountry('usm_mister_rebel').GetName] have declared their intention to conduct military, fiscal and diplomatic affairs in their own government’s name. They fought beside the coalition, but now intend to retain their own rule.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('usm_mister_rebel').GetName] fought beside the coalition. No sooner was the Second Jingnan War over than they sent us a declaration of independence: they refuse to swear allegiance to the new central government at Nanjing that we represent, and mean to run their own army, finances and diplomacy.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('usm_mister_rebel').GetName] has sent an envoy to swear allegiance and recognise the new centre. The wartime partnership has become a relationship of allegiance, under which local civil and military affairs will now be conducted.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('usm_mister_rebel').GetName] has sent envoys to Nanjing to swear allegiance to the new central government. Having weighed strength and popular standing, they have traded the comradeship of the war for the bond between sovereign and subject; local civil and military affairs will now run under the terms newly agreed.

before: The Southern civil war has brought Kyushu back to the centre of Japanese politics. Zheng ports, trade routes and garrisons on the island support Wu’s maritime power and affect the interests of Japanese lords and merchants.\n\nBoth Wu and its opponents seek Japanese intervention, offering to return the Zheng-held parts of Kyushu after victory. The side we support will determine our allies across the sea and the government from which we must claim our reward.
after: The Zheng and the rulers of Japan are old acquaintances. Truth be told, they have long been the masters of China in all but name; by the precedents of Chinese history, a master of the realm taking one step further would be nothing new, and if anything the Zheng have waited a long time.\n\nNow Wu and the provinces against it have both sent men across the sea to ask Japan for troops, and both offer the same price: the return of the Zheng-held parts of Kyushu after the war. Such a chance comes once in a hundred years.

before: Support Wu in exchange for its Kyushu holdings after the war.
after: We need leaders loyal to Shenzhou.

before: Join Wu’s opponents and seek Kyushu through victory.
after: Support those who stand against Wu!

before: Remain neutral and make no military commitment.
after: Perhaps our era has not yet arrived...

Reform now threatens the estates and titles of gentry, former feudal lords and officers; hostile verses and threatening letters continue to arrive. Master Dongguan remains absorbed in public affairs, but the cabinet cannot entrust his safety entirely to old alliances.

The court may fund a personal guard, keep him at his residence, or investigate his attendants and contacts. Protecting the leader of reform will cost money and place more power in the hands of the cabinet directing his guards.

before: Bellandi writes in the newspapers about the girls’ school’s finances, her pupils’ families, and those whom poverty excludes from civic life. Under her questioning, the liberty and independence celebrated by republicans become matters of who pays the fees and who is allowed through the school doors.\n\nSympathetic readers can applaud together in print. For women and the poor to enter the classroom, someone must meet the cost of teaching them, and someone must be willing to let them acquire the power that knowledge brings.
after: Bellandi writes in the newspapers about the girls' school's finances, her pupils' families, and those whom poverty excludes from civic life. Under her questioning, the liberty and independence celebrated by republicans become matters of who pays the fees and who is allowed through the school doors.\n\nHer sympathetic readers cheer as one in print. But before women and the poor can truly walk into a classroom, someone has to pay for the school, and someone has to be willing to let them have the power that learning brings.

before: Whenever Rusciani discusses a common treasury, he returns to the South’s roads and schools. The political centre wants dependable tax revenues, and local traders want dependable trade routes. Both favour cooperation. They disagree over who pays first and who meets the expenses that follow.\n\nRevenue from mining rights has become central to the dispute. If a locality must surrender its income and then wait for others to decide its grants, taxpayers will find little reason to trust the arrangement.
after: Rusciani cannot discuss a common treasury for three sentences without coming back to the South's roads and schools. The political centre wants a dependable tax base; local traders want dependable trade routes. Everyone is for cooperation. The fight is over who pays first, and who carries the costs that keep piling up afterwards.\n\nMining revenue has become the fiercest point of all. Hand over your income first, then wait for others to decide whether to grant you any of it back? The South's taxpayers will not buy that.

before: In the former papal lands, the dispute over education has spread from who may teach children to who will pay their fees. Vitali favours public contributions to school expenses and insists that local churches fulfil their educational responsibilities. This has made him unpopular even among some defenders of the Church’s authority.\n\nThe Church wants to retain its schools, the government wants to educate its citizens, and ordinary families hope their children will learn something useful. These wishes could be reconciled. Yet when it comes to teachers’ wages and poor pupils’ fees, nobody wants to bear a little more of the cost.
after: In the former papal lands, the dispute over education has spread from who may teach children to who will pay their fees. Vitali favours public contributions to school expenses and insists that local churches fulfil their educational responsibilities. This has made him unpopular even among some defenders of the Church's authority.\n\nThe Church wants to keep its schools, the government wants to raise citizens, and ordinary families just want their children to learn something useful. None of these wishes need clash; but the moment it comes to teachers' wages and poor pupils' fees, no one will part with a single coin more.

before: Tong Shiheng’s proposal ties public works closely to commercial interests. Ports want more goods from the interior, merchants want a steady return on their investment, and local communities want roads to reach the places they need. Sometimes these wishes coincide. Sometimes they differ considerably.\n\nA willingness to advance money is therefore not enough to settle the argument. The length of a concession and the distribution of its returns will determine which works merchants consider worth starting, and what transport will cost local people thereafter.
after: Tong Shiheng's proposal ties the works to the merchants' interests. The ports want more goods from the interior, the merchants want a steady return on what they put in, and the towns want the road to reach their own doors. The three hopes sometimes run together and sometimes do not.\n\nSo the merchants' willingness to advance the money does not settle the argument. How long the concession runs and how its returns are shared will decide which works they are willing to start, and how much the towns will pay to move their goods for years afterwards.

before: Port merchants and inland contractors are still seeking long concessions. Tong Shiheng’s proposal for private advances offers the government a chance to save ready cash. Traders along the routes fear that they will pay far more in freight charges later. Both sides want the roads built soon, and both would prefer someone else to bear more of the cost.
after: Port merchants and inland contractors are still seeking long concessions. Tong Shiheng's proposal for private advances would spare the government some ready cash, but traders along the routes fear they will pay far more in freight later.

before: Bayantu insists that local negotiations follow the routes of migrating herds. Contractors can put a price on occupied land. Herders must work out where their animals can go once a passage is lost. If an alternative route lacks water and grass, a payment may do little to restore their livelihood.\n\nSome people await the profits of construction, while others depend on the paths it occupies. These families ask that local plans take their lives into account as well.
after: Bayantu insists that local negotiations follow the routes of migrating herds. Contractors can put a price on occupied land. Herders must work out where their animals can go once a passage is lost. If an alternative route lacks water and grass, a payment may do little to restore their livelihood.\n\nThese families ask that when the district does its sums, their lives be counted too.

before: Guan Tingxian has brought the producing districts’ demands into the budget debate. Oil companies want to use their returns to expand, while local traders need roads and schools for their businesses and families. If each distribution must wait until the companies have arranged their next investments, the districts will always receive what is left over.\n\nHe is therefore demanding both a source of revenue and a local voice in its distribution.
after: Guan Tingxian has brought the producing districts' demands into the budget debate. Oil companies want to use their returns to expand, while local traders need roads and schools for their businesses and families. If each distribution must wait until the companies have arranged their next investments, the districts will always receive what is left over.\n\nWhat he wants is not just a sum of money, but a voice for the districts when the money is shared out.

before: Duan Jingchuan’s concerns about the curriculum always return to his students’ prospects. Academies can teach practical subjects, and local communities need these skills. Students also hope their knowledge will help qualify them to participate in affairs of state.\n\nWhen teaching and examinations value different things, teachers are caught between them. Their pupils’ futures lie on one side, the weight of existing qualifications on the other. The places and recognition Duan seeks must open a workable path between the two.
after: Duan Jingchuan's concerns about the curriculum always return to his students' prospects. Academies can teach practical subjects, and local communities need these skills. Students also hope their knowledge will help qualify them to participate in affairs of state.\n\nThe classroom and the examination hall each weigh things differently, and the teachers are caught in the middle. The students' futures hang on qualifications; Duan fights for places and recognition so that what is taught in the classroom will count in the examination hall.

before: Xu Tingzhang’s opposition to arbitrary levies has found an echo among the local gentry. They will not willingly see their property consumed by post-war finances, or their qualifications diminished in the name of practical learning.\n\nYet local schools must still operate, and military expenses must still be met. Those who defend the old order and wish to continue directing local affairs cannot confine themselves to saying which funds are untouchable and which people must be excluded. Public finance is putting Xu’s position to the test.
after: Xu Tingzhang's opposition to arbitrary levies has found an echo among the local gentry. They will not willingly see their property consumed by post-war finances, or their qualifications diminished in the name of practical learning.\n\nYet local schools must still be run, and the army must still be paid. If the defenders of the old order want to go on running local affairs, they cannot simply list which funds may not be touched and which people may not be let in.

before: Luo Yingtang approaches education through the accounts familiar to women workers. Reading wage statements and invoices helps them speak for themselves in the workshop, and shows them other responsibilities they could undertake. The demand for learning has thus reached the question of qualifications: once they have learned, what may they do?\n\nLiteracy teaching is spreading from workshops to schools. Existing distinctions of status and qualification may prove less flexible. Luo’s concerns now extend to how much opportunity these new skills can bring their students.
after: Luo Yingtang begins her case for education with the accounts women workers know well. Being able to read wage slips and invoices gives them a voice in the workshop, and shows them they could take on other work. And so the demand for learning runs into the question of qualifications: once they have learned, what are they allowed to do?\n\nLiteracy teaching has spread from the workshops to the schools, but the old lines of status and qualification may not loosen with it.

before: Craftsmen and employers both favour teaching skills, but have different plans for the cost of the schools. Employers hope to find more capable workers. Workers hope to earn more once trained. Han Shiduo once brought education and wages into the same discussion. The disputes over both have consequently remained together in the workshops.
after: Employers want more skilled workers; workers want more pay once they are trained; and so the cost of the school is pushed back and forth between them. Han Shiduo once talked about education and wages in the same breath, and now the two quarrels have stayed in the workshops together.

before: Back military works and provide construction assistance to domestic workshops.
after: Get the army's supplies under way first, and the workshops will have orders enough.

before: Public Military Works: Support and Opposition
after: Army First in Line for Contracts

before: Support merchant credit for workshops and direct public funds towards local industry.
after: Let the merchants raise credit for the workshops. A mill opens only when someone can lend the money.

before: Support schools maintained with local contributors.
after: Bring the townsfolk who pay into running the schools, and their own children will have a place to study.

before: Local School Partnerships: Support and Opposition
after: Townsfolk Fund the Schools

before: French support for the Lombard Republic gave the republican cause a foothold in Italy. Orders for workshops, credit for merchants and funds for schools must still be found within Italy. The army presses for military works, merchants seek dependable repayment, and local contributors want places for their children. The government’s spending will help determine whose needs take priority.
after: France's patronage of the Lombard Republic has given the republican cause in Italy something to lean on. But the orders for the workshops, the merchants' credit and the money for local schools must still be found by Italians themselves. The army wants military works first, the merchants want loans with a fixed term, and the townsfolk who fund the schools want a place for their own children.

before: Back pooled revenue and strengthen fiscal administration in the selected state.
after: Gather the taxes in one place, and common undertakings can finally be paid for.

before: Pool Tax Revenue: Support and Opposition
after: Taxes Pooled at the Centre

before: Support local education funding and give the case for retained revenue a basis in school services.
after: Let each state keep its school money, and the schools will open on its own doorstep.

before: Local Revenue and Schools: Support and Opposition
after: States Keep Taxes for Schools

before: Back public works for military expenditure and veterans, with assistance for local military construction.
after: Count army pay and the settlement of veterans among the public works as well.

before: Military Accounts and Veterans: Support and Opposition
after: Army Pay Comes First

before: Building a common Italy means reckoning with the states’ existing military obligations and taxes. Industrial interests favour pooled resources. Local traders want revenue kept for schools, and the army puts military accounts and veterans first. A common budget must reconcile these burdens, whether the states pursue unification or negotiate a lasting relationship among themselves.
after: Before Italy can come together, someone must settle the accounts of each state's armies and taxes. The industrialists want resources pooled, local traders want to keep the money for schools, and the army puts military pay and veterans first. Whether the states bargain one by one or unite at a stroke, there is no way round the question of who controls the revenue.

before: Back chartered contractors with assistance for local construction.
after: Hand the ports and roads to the big contractors and build them with their capital.

before: Chartered Contractors: Support and Opposition
after: Big Contractors Take the Works

before: Support open tenders and assist local transport infrastructure.
after: Put the works out to open tender, so the small firms get their share of the jobs.

before: Open Tenders: Support and Opposition
after: Small Firms Win Tenders

before: Support transport links serving rural communities and local trade.
after: Run the branch lines out to the country market towns first.

before: Local Transport Funds: Support and Opposition
after: Branch Lines to Market Towns First

before: The overseas trade associated with Dongqing depends on routes linking ports with inland timber, minerals and farm produce. Large contractors offer capital through concessions that would also deepen their hold on local trade. Smaller firms seek open tenders, while rural communities want connections to their own towns. The government must decide whose needs will shape the continental roads.
after: Dongqing trades across the ocean, and its ports must be linked to inland timber, ore and farm produce. The big contractors bring capital, but they bring concessions with it, and the districts they serve will come to depend on them. Smaller firms want open tenders, and the countryside wants branch lines run to its own market towns first.

before: Support passage for pastoral communities. Local infrastructure receives assistance, while construction bears the cost of accommodating pasture routes.
after: Leave a path for the herds. The works must detour around the pasture routes and will go more slowly.

before: Protect Pasture Routes: Support and Opposition
after: Pasture Routes Kept Open

before: Support compensated development, improving local infrastructure while accepting slower construction.
after: Pay a fair price for the land taken. The road will get built, but it will take longer.

before: Compensated Development: Support and Opposition
after: Land Bought at a Fair Price

before: Back the army’s proposal to support construction through frontier garrisons.
after: Station troops along the works, and the road will get built.

before: Garrisons for Construction: Support and Opposition
after: Garrisons Guard the Line

before: Railways and mines are reaching into pasture used for seasonal migration. Herds need water and passage; developers need land, and the army wants secure communications. Pastoral communities seek protected routes, developers press for compensated development, and military advocates propose garrisons to support construction. Each course places a different burden on the people who live there.
after: Railways and mines are pushing into the pastures. The blanks on the map are crossed by herds every year: the animals need water, the works need land, and the garrisons need secure roads. The herders want the routes left open, the developers press for land bought outright, and the army proposes troops to guard the works.

before: Support education for workers and families bound by debt through school services in the selected state.
after: Put the children of debt-bound families, and the workers themselves, into school.

before: Labour and Learning: Support and Opposition
after: Debtors' Children in School

before: Back scrutiny of public works accounts and assist local fiscal administration.
after: Lay out every coin spent on the public works for all to see.

before: Publish Public Accounts: Support and Opposition
after: Works Accounts Made Public

before: Families bound by debt bring old obligations and inherited rank with them into the workshops. Teachers and workers seek access to learning. Local traders demand to know who benefits from public expenditure. Support for education and scrutiny of public accounts offer different ways into a dispute over freedom and standing that now reaches into everyday working life.
after: The sons of debt-bound families have come into the workshops, and their old debts, their inherited rank and the dependence they cannot shake off have come in with them. Teachers and workers want a chance to learn; local traders want to know whose pockets the public works money went into. The argument over freedom and standing has landed in the schoolroom and the workshop.

before: Back oil concessions and assist construction serving the oil industry.
after: Grant the drilling rights as concessions and let the companies sink new wells with their profits.

before: Oil Concessions: Support and Opposition
after: Concession Companies Expand

before: Support the case for local oil royalties and assist fiscal administration in the producing state.
after: Keep the oil revenue where the oil comes from, and spend it on roads and schools.

before: Local Oil Royalties: Support and Opposition
after: Oil Revenue Stays Local

before: Back workers’ demands for public oversight of oil and direct local assistance towards education.
after: Let the workers' organisations watch over the wells, and put the local assistance into schools.

before: Public Oil Oversight: Support and Opposition
after: Unions Watch the Wells

before: As oil reaches the market, its proceeds become a question of local power. Concessionary companies want to finance further expansion, traders seek royalties for roads and schools, and workers’ organisations demand public oversight. The government must fund the course it chooses as well as count the revenue promised by the wells.
after: The wells have struck oil, and where the money goes has become local politics. The concession companies want to plough the profits into further expansion, the traders want the royalties kept for roads and schools, and the workers' organisations want the whole industry brought into the open under public oversight.

before: Support classical learning as the basis of public qualifications and strengthen local fiscal administration.
after: Classical learning is the foundation of office. That must not be touched.

before: Retain Classical Examinations: Support and Opposition
after: Classical Gentry Secured

before: Back recognition of practical and commercial learning through assistance to local education.
after: A man who understands machines and can keep accounts deserves a road into office too.

before: Admit Practical and Commercial Learning: Support and Opposition
after: Practical Men Enter Office

before: Support wider provincial places and assist the education of prospective candidates.
after: Give the provinces more examination places, so their sons have a chance to rise.

before: Broaden Provincial Places: Support and Opposition
after: More Provincial Places

before: The Assembly of Rites draws candidates trained in the classics alongside men versed in machinery, accounts and trade. The cabinet and Six Ministries seek capable officials, while the provinces press the claims of their own students. The weight given to classical qualifications, practical learning and provincial places will shape access to public life under the Constitution and the standing of the established gentry.
after: At the doors of the Assembly of Rites stand scholars versed in the classics, and beside them newcomers who understand machinery, accounts and trade. The cabinet and Six Ministries want capable men from among them, and every province wants to know whether its own sons will be chosen. How much weight goes to classical qualifications, practical experience and provincial places decides who may enter public life under the Constitution, and puts the old gentry's standing in question.

before: Support practical curricula in the academies and assist their teaching.
after: Add practical courses to the academies, and the teachers' salaries will be found.

before: Practical Curricula: Support and Opposition
after: Academies Teach Practical Learning

before: Support wider provincial access to learning through local school services.
after: Give the provinces more school places, so the village youth have books to read.

before: Provincial Places: Support and Opposition
after: More Places for Local Youth

before: Academy teachers must make room for surveying, machinery and commercial learning alongside the classics. Students seek useful knowledge and a chance to qualify for the Assembly of Rites examinations. Provincial administrators must find the money; provincial delegates bring demands for curricula and places into national debate. Practical teaching and wider provincial access compete for the same education funds.
after: The academy teachers lecture on the classics; their students want surveying, machinery and commercial learning. The students hope to learn something useful, and hope even more to qualify for the Assembly of Rites examinations. Provincial administrators have to find the money, and provincial delegates carry each province's demands for courses and places into national politics. Practical courses and provincial places are fighting over the same education budget.

before: Assist construction and industrial operations in coastal workshops.
after: Put the money into the coastal works first. That is where the ports and shipping lanes are.

before: Coastal Workshops: Support and Opposition
after: Coastal Mill Owners Ascendant

before: Direct industrial investment inland and assist local workshop operations through infrastructure.
after: Industry cannot stop at the coast. The interior needs roads and works of its own.

before: Inland Industry: Support and Opposition

before: Coastal merchants look to ports and shipping when establishing workshops. Inland towns also seek industrial investment, while provincial administrators must answer for local taxes and construction costs. Machinery, labour and goods cross provincial boundaries more readily than those obligations. The government’s choice of where to invest must eventually be borne out in the operation of the works.
after: Coastal merchants set up their workshops along the ports and shipping lanes, and the inland towns hold out their hands for investment too. Machinery, labour and goods must move between provinces, yet each provincial administrator sees only his own province's taxes and building costs. Prosperity in memorials to the throne counts for nothing; only works that keep running show where the money went.

before: Support concentrated commercial investment and assist industrial construction in the selected state.
after: Concentrate the investment where trade already thrives, and put the best steel to the sharpest edge.

before: Back broader qualifications for provincial delegates through assistance to local education.
after: Widen the qualifications for provincial delegates and let more scholars into the Assembly of Rites.

before: Revenue from industry and trade may return to prosperous commercial centres or support public works across the provinces. The cabinet and Six Ministries plan expenditure; delegates in the Assembly of Rites must answer for what their provinces contribute and receive. Commercial investment, provincial development and access to public office now contend over the gains of industrial growth.
after: New works and new shipping have brought in new revenue. It can be poured back into the thriving commercial centres, or shared among the provinces for public works. The cabinet and Six Ministries plan the spending; the provincial delegates in the Assembly of Rites must answer for what their provinces paid in and what they got back. The constitutional quarrel over shares now has a fresh pot of money to fight over.

before: The undertaking has stood the test of ordinary operation. The services or production supported by the expenditure now offer tangible results, giving local debate over costs and benefits something concrete to judge.
after: The works have survived their first months and settled into everyday operation. The services and production that the money paid for are showing real results, and the long local argument over costs and returns finally has accounts to check.

Provincial administrators execute fiscal administration, while provincial delegates represent their provinces. Academy students learn useful arts and prepare for the Assembly’s examinations. Expanding schools and industry sharpens the dispute over who may enter public life and who must pay.
after: The cabinet and Six Ministries propose new measures, the Assembly of Rites debates the Constitution, provincial administrators run finance and government, and provincial delegates speak for their provinces in national affairs. Academy students learn their trades while preparing for the Assembly's examinations. The more schools and industries open, the louder the quarrel over who may enter office and who must pay.

before: A neighbouring state proposes a shared public undertaking. Schools, local revenues and military expenses would become budgetary obligations for both governments. Each must fund services on its own territory. The proposal preserves both states and their borders; the decision is ours.
after: A neighbouring state proposes that we share the burden of public works. Schools, local taxes and army costs would no longer be fine words in speeches about unity: each country would pay from its own treasury and get the work done on its own soil. The proposal leaves both governments and both territories untouched.

before: Accept the mutual obligations.
after: Each pays its share, and what we agreed gets done.

before: Ask for schools and local services first.
after: Schools and local services come first.

before: Decline the proposal.
after: We will not sign up to this bill.

before: The other government is willing to cooperate but asks that schools and local services take priority over military supply. If we agree, both countries will fund these undertakings and maintain the services within their own borders.
after: The other side will cooperate, on condition that the money goes to schools and local services rather than military supply. If we agree, both countries fund these undertakings, each running the services within its own borders.

before: Accept the proposed priorities.
after: Schools first, then. So be it.

before: The states have failed to settle the obligations of this undertaking. Each remains responsible for its schools, revenue and military expenditure; further talks must await another occasion.
after: The states could not agree on this term's public obligations. Schools, taxes and army costs remain each state's own business.

before: Both countries have fulfilled the agreement, funding and providing the promised educational, administrative or military services. Cooperation has created shared interests in the provinces and built trust for further negotiations.
after: Both countries have kept their word, each finding the money and the people for its schools, administration or military supply. Having made cooperation work once, the next round of talks should come easier.

before: Let the accord take root.
after: Carry on as we have begun.

before: Western provincial integration has failed; remaining schools and industry still require support.
after: Western provincial integration has failed. The schools and industries we already run will be kept going.

before: The Italian states have different governments, armies and foreign ties. The Lombard Republic endures with French support, while republican conviction, dynastic interests and local finances shape the road ahead. The states may pursue unification or lasting cooperation through public obligations.
after: Each Italian state has its own government, army and foreign ties. The Lombard Republic has France at its back, and republicans, dynasties and local purse-holders all want to point the way to unity. Some want a single Italy; others want no more than lasting cooperation on public obligations.

before: Italian political mobilisation has changed local government. Established republics and newly organised republican forces seek cooperation, while military costs, revenue and representation remain matters for concrete negotiation.
after: Political mobilisation has stirred up local politics across Italy. Old republics and newly organised republicans are courting allies, but nothing is settled: not how to share army costs, not how to raise taxes, not how to choose representatives.

before: Italy’s future is debated in schools, barracks and state governments. Support for unification need not entail hostility to France; protection cannot answer local questions of revenue and political standing.
after: Everyone is arguing over Italy's future: in the schools, in the barracks, in the councils of every state. Unity need not mean a quarrel with France; but how to divide the revenue, and who has the right to sit in council, are questions French protection cannot answer for the Italians.
