before: Current law has ended slavery and provides protection for assembly or speech. Debt bonds no longer govern a life in their former fashion, while education, occupations and social standing remain disputed. The consequences of the registration order do not disappear automatically.
after: Slavery is abolished, and assembly and speech are protected by law. A debt bond can no longer rule a person's whole life as it once did. But what the registration order left behind will not vanish overnight: who may study, who may take up which trade, who counts as what — the republic will have to fight over each in turn.

before: The southern government asks Duan Jingchuan to discuss academy curricula and educational places. Sichuan is independent; this invitation requires its own decision. The teacher’s home and the affairs of local schools remain under this government.
after: The southern government has asked Duan Jingchuan to join its discussions on academy curricula and places. Sichuan is independent now; Nanjing can no longer summon a man with a provincial order as it once did. Whether he goes is for us to decide.

before: Allow a scholarly exchange.
after: Let him make the journey.

before: Keep the teacher at home.
after: Sichuan's teachers stay in Sichuan.

before: Independent Sichuan has agreed to a scholarly exchange with the southern government. Curricula and educational places offer a basis for contact between their academies, while each state retains its own schools. Qualifications for the Assembly of Rites remain subject to its examinations and constitutional procedures.
after: Sichuan has agreed to the teacher exchange. The academies on both sides can keep up regular contact on curricula and places, while each runs its own schools. Qualification for the Assembly of Rites still depends on the southern government's own examinations and constitutional procedures.

before: No plan is currently underway for this undertaking.
after: No plan has been chosen for this undertaking

before: An implementation plan has been chosen for this undertaking.
after: A plan has been chosen for this undertaking

before: This country seeks changes to land tenure and wider public education. Political support, administrative capacity and the normal legislative process govern its progress.
after: This country plans to change land tenure and widen public education. How fast it goes depends on political support, administrative capacity and the legislative process.

before: Military nobles and local lineages hold estates that bind farming families to old patrons. Marketable land opens agriculture to new investment, but a sale does not provide a livelihood for those displaced. Employment and migration must follow the change in ownership.
after: The estates amassed by military nobles and local lineages have kept generations of farming families bound to their old masters. The new law lets land change hands, and gives merchant farmers room to expand. But a bill of sale cannot conjure up a new living for those who lose their land. The quarrels over converted estates, hired labour and resettlement will follow this change into every village.

before: Suspend the state-sponsored resettlement and urban expansion programme.
after: Suspend state resettlement and urban expansion, and withdraw this grant.

before: Since 1444, the Qin military colonies of Northern Ming have developed into an estate system across the north. Land supplied the army's food and pay, while the army sustained taxation and conquest. Military and agricultural interests grew together. Bringing these lands and mines into civilian use now threatens entrenched military privileges.\n\nThe Ministry of Revenue wants the estates brought under ordinary taxation and management. The Ministry of War must answer officers who invoke unpaid wages and past service. Governors charged with enforcing the law may lack the force to compel their garrisons, while the founding commanders in the Senate are reluctant to surrender their own property. The provinces can proceed separately and suspend reform where disputes become unmanageable. New revenue and production must eventually replace the army's landed income.
after: Since 1444, the Qin military colonies of Northern Ming have developed into an estate system across the north. Land supplied the army's food and pay, while the army sustained taxation and conquest. Military and agricultural interests grew together. Bringing these lands and mines into civilian use now threatens entrenched military privileges.\n\nThe Ministry of Revenue wants every province to bring the estates under ordinary taxation and management; the Ministry of War, meanwhile, has to fend off generals demanding back pay and rewards for old service. It is the governors who must enforce the new law, yet they may not have the troops to overawe the garrisons. The founding commanders in the Senate will not lightly agree to be stripped of their own property either. In the end, the land the army loses must be made up by new revenue and new production.

before: The governor of [SCOPE.sState('nesnd_cne_funding_state').GetName] reports that many people leaving the estates lack the skills needed by workshops and struggle to find a living in town. The Ministry of Revenue proposes a grant for practical schools and workshop expansion. Learning a new trade would give these families the means to use the freedom promised by land reform.
after: The governor of [SCOPE.sState('nesnd_cne_funding_state').GetName] reports that many people leaving the estates lack the skills needed by workshops and struggle to find a living in town. The Ministry of Revenue proposes a grant for practical schools and workshop expansion. Only when these villagers have learned a new trade will the freedom promised by land reform have something to stand on.

before: Zheng fleets, trading houses and dependencies have carried news of the Southern war abroad. Merchants fear the seizure of their cargoes, while envoys from the rival sides seek recognition, military supplies and loans.\n\n[ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] has interests of its own in these exchanges. Keeping trade open requires dealings with those who control the ports and sea routes. Receiving exiles or supplying the anti-Wu forces would draw us more deeply into the Southern political struggle.
after: Zheng fleets, trading houses and dependencies have carried news of the Southern war abroad. Merchants fear the seizure of their cargoes, while envoys from the rival sides seek recognition, military supplies and loans.\n\n[ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] has its own calculations in all this. Keeping trade open means dealing with whoever actually holds the ports and sea lanes; sheltering exiles or supplying the anti-Wu forces would bind the South's old and new powers more tightly to us.

before: With the fighting ended, local civil and military authority is passing under Wu rule. The new dynasty must now govern: production and trade disrupted by war must recover, people need their livelihoods, and officials and scholars who opposed Zheng will not disappear with defeat.\n\nHangzhou’s accumulated military and fiscal strength can sustain reconstruction. We may judge opponents individually and retain experienced local officials, or use victory to purge the old parties and make the army the foundation of the new order. These decisions will show the realm what government in the Zheng family’s own name means.
after: The fighting is over, and local civil and military authority is passing to Wu one province after another. The question now is how to govern: production and trade broken by war must recover, the people of every province must go on living, and the officials and scholars who opposed the Zheng will not vanish with their defeat.\n\nThe army and treasury Hangzhou has built up over the years can pay for the rebuilding. From the first few decrees, the realm will learn what kind of court the Zheng mean to run in their own name.

before: The troops are returning from abroad. Local lords demand the rewards promised when they joined the campaign, merchants want shipping restored, and the government must arrange its garrisons and revenues.\n\nThe mainland war has given [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] an opportunity to reorganise. More consistent taxation and official training would strengthen central administration. Honouring military claims first would secure the commanders and lords on whom the expedition relied.
after: The troops are returning from abroad. Local lords demand the rewards promised when they joined the campaign, merchants want shipping restored, and the government must arrange its garrisons and revenues.\n\nThe mainland war has handed [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] a chance to put its army and government in order.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] proposes a military alliance with a five-year binding period. Its envoy links the security of the German states to the continental order dominated by France and asks us to share the risks of diplomacy and war.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] wants a military alliance with us for a five-year binding period. Its envoy binds the safety of the German states to the continental order France dominates, and asks us to stand with them in diplomacy and on the battlefield from now on.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] proposes a defensive pact with a five-year binding period. It seeks a practical safeguard for national independence and expects both governments to fulfil their obligations if either is attacked.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] proposes a defensive pact with a five-year binding period. What they want is an agreement that truly protects their independence: if either side is attacked, the other marches.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] asks France to lend political credit to its Italian programme for six years. Its supporters hope French prestige will persuade domestic and foreign interests to accept the undertaking. The commitment itself does not alter the sovereignty of the Italian states.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] asks France to stand guarantor for its Italian programme with six years of political credit. With French prestige behind them, its supporters can win over interests at home and abroad. The commitment does not touch the sovereignty of the Italian states.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] offers our investors access under an agreement with a five-year binding period. It hopes to attract factories and expertise while accepting the disputes over income and influence that foreign capital can bring. The agreement grants investment rights; construction remains a business decision.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] offers to open its market to our investors under an agreement with a five-year binding period. They want new factories and new expertise, and are ready to handle the scramble over profits that foreign capital brings. The agreement grants the right to invest; whether firms actually build depends on the business.

before: We cannot undertake this commitment.
after: This is a commitment we cannot carry.

before: The other government has accepted the terms, and the agreed undertaking is now in place. Further cooperation will depend on both countries continuing to fulfil their obligations.
after: The other government has accepted the terms of our letter, and the agreed commitment now stands.

before: These negotiations have produced no effective agreement. The other government either withheld its commitment or circumstances changed before the original terms could be settled. The envoy will return with that outcome.
after: The talks came to nothing. Either the other side refused, or events changed during the negotiations and the original terms no longer held. The envoy returns empty-handed.

before: The agreement of 1825 recognized Egypt's independence from Ottoman rule. Six powers guaranteed that independence in exchange for investment rights along the Nile. The government gained a respite, but its workshops, schools and army grew dependent on foreign money and expertise.\n\nAn investment partner can provide machinery, teachers and new industries. As foreign ownership grows, Egypt has less room to act on its own. Over the next thirty years, the government must weigh development against independence.
after: The agreement of 1825 recognised Egypt's independence from Ottoman rule, and six powers guaranteed it in return for the right to invest along the Nile. The court won a breathing space, but its workshops, schools and army came to lean on foreign money and expertise.\n\nAn investment partner brings machines, teachers and new industries. Yet the more the foreigners own, the less Egypt can decide for itself. This is how it must live for thirty years.

before: Egypt will bear political responsibility for its own development.
after: Egypt will walk its own road.

before: For thirty years, Egypt has preserved its own government and control of its foreign affairs. Foreign merchants still operate along the Nile, and the powers still pursue their interests here, but they have not gained the right to decide Egypt's affairs. Our schools and workshops will continue to sustain that independence.
after: Thirty years have passed, and Egypt has kept its own government and its own foreign policy. Foreign merchants still trade along the Nile, and the powers have not given up their schemes here, but Egypt's affairs have never been theirs to decide.

before: The government must answer for this.
after: This burden is ours alone to bear.

before: Graduates are entering the workshops, and toolmakers and new industries have established a steady workforce. Egypt is developing its own capacity to teach and manufacture, with more local engineers and workers able to take part in its development.
after: Graduates of the university are entering the workshops, and the toolmakers and new industries now have a steady workforce. In the building still to come, more and more of the engineers and workers will be Egyptians.

before: France and the Confederation of the Rhine sustain the division of the German states. To challenge their influence, Prussia must convince other governments that Berlin will commit its army to their common interests.\n\nAlliances and defensive pacts can bring the states together, but troops and armaments must sustain those commitments. Governments still bound to France or a Rhenish overlord need freedom in foreign affairs before they can join.
after: France and the Confederation of the Rhine keep the German states apart. If Prussia is to contest their influence, it must convince the other states that Berlin will put its army behind their common interests.\n\nAlliances and defensive pacts tie the states together, and it is the army and the arsenals that make the promises good. States still answering to France or a Rhenish overlord must win back their freedom in foreign affairs before they can join.

before: Republicans supported by France, the ruling dynasties and the Pope all seek to shape Italy's future. Austria can support independent states through defensive pacts or intervene to prevent their annexation.\n\nIntervention requires money and allies. Accepting the advance of a unifying power would mean accepting a diminished Austrian influence in Italy.
after: French-backed republicans, the ruling dynasties and the Pope all want to decide Italy's future. Austria can prop up the independent states with defensive pacts, or send troops to stop them being swallowed.\n\nIntervention takes money, and allies. If Vienna accepts the unifiers' gains, its word will carry far less weight in Italy.

before: The old order through which France dominated the German states has receded. Prussia has gained influence in the struggle, and the military and diplomatic ties forged along the way will continue to shape the states' decisions.
after: The old order under which France ruled the German states is ebbing away. Prussia has come out of the contest with more weight, and the military and diplomatic ties it formed along the way will go on pulling at the states' choices.

before: Austria has joined the defending side in the Italian dispute. Diplomatic assurances now carry military and financial commitments, and Vienna’s prestige will share in the outcome.
after: Austria has taken the defending side in the Italian dispute. The envoys' promises now have troops and money behind them, and Vienna's prestige is staked on how the dispute ends.

before: Austria’s intervention has failed to preserve the position it sought to defend. Territorial demands, subordination or the disappearance of the protected state have undone the original commitment. Vienna must face the consequences in Italy.
after: Austria's intervention has failed to save what it set out to save. Territorial demands, a change of allegiance or the end of the protected state have left the original promise hollow. Every Italian state will remember this failure.

before: The dispute has ended without a result Austria can claim as a victory. The protected state survives, but the disagreement has not been decisively settled. Both sides must consider their next course.
after: The dispute is over, and Austria has nothing to show that it could call a victory. The protected state survives, but not one of the disagreements has been settled.

before: The United States has demanded [SCOPE.sState('nesnd_usa_disputed_state').GetName]. Federal envoys call it the restoration of a rightful border; residents, landowners and the garrison face an immediate contest over sovereignty. Our government must decide its response through the diplomatic play now before it.
after: The United States has demanded [SCOPE.sState('nesnd_usa_disputed_state').GetName]. The federal envoys call it restoring a rightful border; for the residents, landowners and garrison, it is a hard fight over sovereignty.

before: Citizenship has never carried equal weight in the $HUS$. Han residents stand first, followed by Manchu and Mongol peoples, Indigenous Americans, and Europeans. Living in the same republic does not bring the same treatment. The question of widening the civic body has now reached the government. Manchu and Mongol residents seek equality through their ties with the Han. Indigenous peoples demand recognition of their claims upon this land and its republic.\n\nThe government will grant first-tier registration to one of these groups after a year of registration. Its decision will also reshape relations with those left under the old distinctions.
after: Citizenship has never carried the same weight for everyone in the $HUS$. The Han come first, then Manchu and Mongol residents, Indigenous Americans and Europeans in turn: one country, but treatment divided into ranks. Now the argument over widening citizenship has reached the government. The Manchu and Mongols claim equality through their old ties to the Han; Indigenous peoples demand that the republic recognise their share in this land and this country.\n\nThe government can raise only one of them to first-tier registration, with the new law taking effect after a year of registration. Those left in the old ranks will remember this choice.

before: Manchu and Mongol residents now share first-tier registration with the Han. Indigenous Americans remain in the third tier and Europeans in the fourth. The republic has extended its highest civic standing while retaining distinctions between registrations.
after: Manchu and Mongol residents now share first-tier registration with the Han. Indigenous Americans remain in the third tier and Europeans in the fourth. The ranks still stand; the first rank has simply grown larger.

before: Indigenous Americans now share first-tier registration with the Han. Manchu and Mongol residents remain in the second tier and Europeans in the fourth. The republic has granted Indigenous residents equal standing with the Han while leaving Manchu and Mongol communities under the old hierarchy.
after: Indigenous Americans now share first-tier registration with the Han. Manchu and Mongol residents remain in the second tier and Europeans in the fourth. The Manchu and Mongols have been left behind in the old hierarchy.

before: Our decision has become law.
after: The new law stands.

before: Ties between Manchu, Mongol, and Han residents offer one path to a broader civic body. The government will recognize their equal social standing.
after: The Manchu and Mongols have deep ties to the Han. Raising them to the first rank is the easiest step towards a wider citizenship.

before: Indigenous peoples share the republic’s land. The government will recognize their equal standing with Han residents, prompting Manchu and Mongol residents left in the second tier to seek a life elsewhere.
after: This land was the Indigenous peoples' home first, and they deserve the same standing as the Han. The Manchu and Mongols left in the second tier will look for a life elsewhere.

before: Living under one government does not make its subjects a nation. The provinces have their own languages, faiths and princes. As schools and cities grow, their inhabitants are asking who can speak for India. Dynasties, local leaders and the emerging national movement must each offer an answer.
after: Living in one country does not make people compatriots. The provinces have their own languages, faiths and princes of old. Now that schools and cities are growing, people have begun to argue: who has the right to speak for India? The dynasty, the local leaders and the rising national movement each have their own answer.

before: Delhi, Nanjing and Paris each have terms to offer the Indian princes. Their rulers seek to preserve more than ancestral palaces: land, revenue and the right to decide their own future are at stake. Cooperation may bring assistance without securing independence.
after: Delhi, Nanjing and Paris have each named their terms to the Indian princes. The princes mean to keep more than their ancestral palaces: their land, their revenue and the fate of their own states. No one's help comes free.

before: France seeks to maintain its influence in India through trade, investment and military aid, while the government in Delhi needs teachers, engineers and officers. French expertise can train local specialists, but relying on it will prolong the country's dependence on Paris.
after: France wants to keep its hold on India through trade, investment and military aid; Delhi is short of teachers, engineers and officers. The specialists trained under French instruction will be our own, but our patron will still be Paris.

before: Foreign assistance calls for a policy of our own.
after: Take France's help, but keep our own counsel.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('india_partner').GetName] has accepted our request. The agreement is now in effect; making good use of it falls to us.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('india_partner').GetName] has accepted our request. The agreement has been put into effect.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('india_partner').GetName] has declined the delegation’s terms. We must seek another way forward.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('india_partner').GetName] has turned down the delegation's terms. We will have to find another way.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('india_sender').GetName] asks France to send teachers and fund the first stages of its education program. The envoys hope to train local specialists, while the mission would extend French influence over education in their country.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('india_sender').GetName] asks France to send teachers and to fund its first few schools. They want specialists of their own; and once French advisers are in the classrooms, France's weight in their education grows too.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('india_sender').GetName] asks France to send mining and industrial engineers and provide funding to establish new industries. The envoys seek production techniques, while French businesses see opportunities in the proposed cooperation.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('india_sender').GetName] asks France to send mining and industrial engineers and to fund new industries. They want the new methods of production; French firms have their eye on the business.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('india_sender').GetName] asks France to send military instructors and help fund the reorganization of its army. The recipient seeks better training and equipment, while France would gain influence over the army's development.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('india_sender').GetName] asks France to send military instructors and help pay to reorganise its army. They want an army worth the name; France would get the chance to set that army's rules for years to come.

before: The envoys of [SCOPE.sCountry('india_sender').GetName] request greater autonomy so that their government can manage more of its own affairs. We must decide whether to relinquish some of our authority as overlord.
after: The envoys of [SCOPE.sCountry('india_sender').GetName] ask for greater autonomy, so that their own government can handle more of its affairs.

before: Opponents of colonial rule in [SCOPE.sState('india_case_state').GetName] have seized the local administration and declared their independence. Recognition of their breakaway government is now a dispute between states.
after: Opponents of colonial rule in [SCOPE.sState('india_case_state').GetName] have risen openly, seized the local offices and declared they no longer obey their old rulers. Whether to recognise the breakaway has become a dispute between two states.

before: The dynasty’s old prestige still carries weight, but its subjects also judge their sovereign by the conduct of government. Respect for the provinces’ faiths and the court’s ability to make its own decisions will shape their loyalty.
after: The dynasty's old prestige still counts, but people also weigh their sovereign by the government in front of them. Whether the provinces' faiths are respected, and whether Delhi can make up its own mind, will decide whether the provinces still stand by this dynasty.

before: The Toyotomi unified Japan with Ming and Wu assistance and fought beside the Zheng in Korea. Their old alliance bound the garrisons in Kyushu to the interests of Japan’s lords. With affairs in the south settled, the court is considering an expedition: send former western officers overseas and establish imperial and Tokugawa governments alongside the Toyotomi, while placing Kyushu and Shikoku under direct Wu administration. The settlement would also reshape overseas garrisons and maritime trade.
after: The Toyotomi ended the Warring States with Ming and Wu help, then fought beside the Zheng for Korea. Generations of alliance have tangled the Kyushu garrisons up with the interests of Japan's lords. Now that the South is settled, the court has begun to talk of an eastern expedition: ship the old western army across the sea, raise up the Emperor and the Tokugawa alongside the Toyotomi, give each of the three houses its own lands, and place Kyushu and Shikoku under direct Wu rule. The overseas garrisons and sea trade would all have to be carved up anew.

before: The envoys have departed for Japan, and the court awaits its reply.
after: The envoys have crossed the sea. No reply has come yet.

before: Keep the current borders and Japanese government; retain resources for the mainland and other overseas commitments.
after: Leave Japan's government and borders as they are. Keep the fleet and the soldiers' pay for the homeland and our other overseas domains.

before: Alliances across the strait once helped the Toyotomi conquer their rivals and allowed the mainland court to intervene in Japan’s successions, domains and wars. Taxes, armies and commerce now follow competing authorities. [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] must reunite Honshu and secure the freedom to govern its own affairs.
after: The alliance across the strait swept away the Toyotomi's rivals, and it also invited the mainland court into Japan's successions, fiefs and wars. Today the taxes of the castle towns flow into many separate treasuries, and every army and merchant answers to a different master. To rebuild a single government, [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] must first bring Honshu together, then take its own affairs, at home and abroad, back into its own hands.

before: The envoys from Nanjing propose to divide the realm. Kyoto and Osaka would recognize the Emperor, the Tokugawa would rule from Edo, and the Toyotomi would govern western Kansai and Chugoku. Wu would administer Kyushu and Shikoku directly. The levies and revenues of the eastern domains would henceforth answer to several governments. The retainers have laid their accounts of troops and provisions before [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName], who must decide how to answer.
after: The envoys from Nanjing have brought a plan to partition the realm: Kyoto and Osaka for the Emperor, Edo for the Tokugawa, the rest of Kansai and the Chugoku region for the Toyotomi, and Kyushu and Shikoku under direct Wu rule. The soldiers and taxes of the eastern domains would be split among several houses. The retainers have laid the muster rolls and grain ledgers before [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName].

before: Japan’s envoys have declined the proposed settlement. An expedition would require Nanjing to provide funds and ships to install the three houses in their domains. The court may also withdraw its demands and leave Japan under a single government. The decision rests with [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName].
after: Japan's envoys have refused the partition. An expedition means raising money and ships and escorting the three houses into their new domains; the alternative is to withdraw the demand and leave Japan united. The envoys' reply now lies before [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName].

before: The conflict has ended without implementation of the partition. Fleets and garrisons will redeploy under the existing borders and agreements.
after: The fighting over the eastern expedition is done, and Japan has not been divided into three. Fleets and garrisons will redeploy along the current borders, and army funds and trade routes must be handed over item by item. Eastern affairs will be handled under the peace treaties now in force.

before: Honshu now answers to one independent government. [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] is bringing the revenues and armies of the former domains under common authority. Merchants in the castle towns await a settlement of tolls and taxes as they prepare to trade beyond the old domain boundaries.
after: At last, all of Honshu answers to one independent government. [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] has taken over the old lords' taxes and armies, and domains that once went their own way now follow a single code of law. The castle-town merchants are waiting for tolls and levies to be settled anew, so they can carry their trade beyond the old domain borders.

before: Japan’s envoys have declined the settlement. [SCOPE.sCharacter('nesnd_japan_commander').GetFullName] has been charged with planning an expedition. Officers of the former western army would sail with their commander, while Nanjing must provide the fleet, pay and reinforcements. The court must decide whether to take up arms or withdraw its proposal.
after: Japan's envoys have refused the partition. [SCOPE.sCharacter('nesnd_japan_commander').GetFullName] has been ordered to plan the expedition; the officers of the old western army are waiting to sail with him, and the fleet, the pay and the domains' auxiliaries must all come from Nanjing. War, or withdraw the partition?

before: Merchants who once bought cotton and silk from scattered households are bringing weavers together in larger mills. Wage work offers a new livelihood to people leaving the land, though it also subjects familiar skills to the discipline of a foreman. For the merchants, it promises closer control over production.
after: Merchants who buy up raw silk and cotton have begun gathering the weavers under one roof. Familiar handwork has moved into bigger mills, where wages come on time and the foreman's rules must be obeyed. People leaving the land have found a new hope; the merchants have tightened their grip on rural production.

before: Food, furniture and household goods are finding customers beyond the wealthiest homes. Their manufacturers have acquired a reason to care about ordinary incomes. Families struggling to feed themselves have little to spend on other goods, limiting sales and putting pressure on prices and profits.
after: The trade in food, furniture and household wares is spreading from a few wealthy houses into many more homes. The men who run these workshops have started to worry about ordinary wages: if customers can barely feed themselves, nothing sells and prices cannot rise.

before: Families who have found work in the mills must still pay rent, buy food and find money for their children’s schooling. They have brought labour and tax revenue to the towns, and expect a share in their prosperity. The promise of a better life will be judged against these everyday expenses.
after: Those who have gone into the mills now reckon up the rent, the price of rice and the cost of their children's schooling. The towns owe their labour and their tax revenue to these people, and they want their own share of the prosperity. Whether the government's promise of a new life holds good will be measured by these few expenses.

before: Harvests, fishing boats and grain merchants sustain life in the towns. When food prices rise, complaints from the markets soon reach the authorities. The government must keep food coming into the towns at prices their people can afford.
after: The harvest, the fishing boats and the grain dealers feed the towns. When grain prices rise, the grumbling in the markets soon reaches the government offices. Only when carriers are willing to bring food in, and townspeople can afford to buy it, will the streets stay calm.

before: The towns need food that can be stored and carried over long distances. Grain and fish merchants want customers beyond the harvest season. Canning offers a way to combine purchasing, processing and transport in one business, while food factories could provide work after the harvest is over.
after: The towns need food that keeps and travels, and the grain and fish dealers want buyers outside the harvest season. Canning lets them join buying, processing and shipping into a single business. With food works open, labourers no longer lose their jobs the moment the harvest ends.

before: The domains of the shogunate, rural clans and merchants of the castle towns once upheld their own local orders. Schools and public administration connect distant communities, while flourishing commerce ties more livelihoods together. Security at home and the country’s fortunes in war shape confidence in a shared future.
after: Under the shogunate, the domains, the rural clans and the castle-town merchants each kept order in their own corner. Now schools and government offices tie near and far together, and trade binds more and more livelihoods to one another. Whether life is secure, and whether the country can protect them in war, the people are watching.

before: After unifying Japan, the Toyotomi advanced into Korea with the Wu ruler's aid and secured their domains to the east. The authority of the Ming court, their own armies and Osaka's financial houses sustained the Taiko shogunate. New wealth and learning are changing these relationships. Merchants, officers and scholars seek a greater say in government. Disputes over appointments, the army and the law now concern who will control the state.
after: After unifying Japan, the Toyotomi advanced into Korea with the Wu ruler's aid and secured their domains to the east. The authority of the Ming court, their own armies and Osaka's financial houses sustained the Taiko shogunate. Now new money and new learning have loosened the old hold on power, and merchants, officers and scholars all want a say in state affairs. The quarrels over appointments, the army and the law come down, in the end, to who will run the government.

before: The old retainers want reform carried out in the monarch’s name. Merchants and officials trained in the new schools seek legal protection from arbitrary levies and local power. The crown can bring them together, but their respective rights remain to be settled.
after: The old retainers want reform carried out in the monarch's name. Merchants and officials schooled in the new learning want the law to shield them from arbitrary levies and local strongmen. The crown's name can bring all these people into one room, but each man's rights must still be drawn up, clause by clause.

before: The promises made in pursuit of independence now confront the government. Who will pay for defence, who will set the tariffs, and how much authority will remain in local hands? Those who contributed money and those who served expect a place in the new state.
after: The promises made in the struggle for independence must now be paid out one by one. Who pays for the army, who sets the tariffs, how far local authority reaches: none of it is settled. Those who gave money and those who gave service are all waiting for their place in the new state.

before: Hereditary warriors and local loyalties sustained the old armies, with recruitment and training varying between domains. The country needs organized manpower, trained officers and forces that answer to a common command. Whether defence rests on a standing army or a national militia, military service must support the affairs of the nation.
after: The old armies rested on hereditary warriors and local ties, and every house recruited and drilled in its own way. The country needs organised recruits, trained officers and forces that answer to a single command.

before: Tributary ties and maritime restrictions once placed diplomacy and trade within an overlord’s arrangements. We need to open our ports, send out merchant ships and negotiate with other countries in our own name. Lasting sovereignty will give these exchanges a government they can rely upon.
after: Tribute and the maritime bans once bound both diplomacy and trade to the overlord's arrangements. Now we must send out merchant ships and open our ports in our own name, and bargain with other countries over our own interests.

before: Japan’s overseas trade has long been confined to a few designated ports by strict prohibitions. Merchants seek distant raw materials and wider markets for their produce. The government must arrange the opening of the ports and confront those whose influence rests on the old restrictions.
after: For many years Japan's overseas trade has been penned into a few ports by strict prohibitions. Merchants want raw materials from afar and wider markets for Japanese goods. Those who have lived off the old bans will not give up the ports easily.

before: Honshu has been reunited, but the question of Kyushu and Shikoku remains unsettled. Their ports and sea routes matter to trade and defence in southern Japan. The government may seek the remaining territories or accept the existing borders and relinquish its claims.
after: Honshu is united, but Kyushu and Shikoku have not all been recovered. Their ports and sea lanes are the gateway to southern Japan's trade and defence.

before: The dynasty can bring loyal retainers and reformers together. Preserve the crown, appoint capable officials, and give representative deliberation and enterprise a place in the state.\n\nThe policy cannot be changed for #v 12#! months. Changing policy resets reform progress.
after: The dynasty's name can gather old retainers and reformers into one camp. The monarch stays on the throne, new officials are appointed all the same, and both deliberation and enterprise are put to work for the country.\n\nThe policy cannot be changed for #v 12#! months. Changing policy resets reform progress.

before: The army needs a common command, and the state needs orders that can be carried through. Back the officers in reorganizing recruitment and supply, drawing provincial manpower and revenues into a common defence.\n\nThe policy cannot be changed for #v 12#! months. Changing policy resets reform progress.
after: The army needs one command, and orders must be carried through to the end. Let the officers reorganise recruitment and supply, and gather the manpower and money of every province into the nation's defence.\n\nThe policy cannot be changed for #v 12#! months. Changing policy resets reform progress.

before: Public affairs concern everyone who pays taxes, serves or earns a living. Bring more representatives into government, subject officials to public debate, and let voters influence the conduct of the state.\n\nThe policy cannot be changed for #v 12#! months. Changing policy resets reform progress.
after: Those who pay taxes, serve in the ranks and earn a living carry the weight of every state affair. Put more representatives in the chamber, and officials will have to answer in public, and citizens will have a vote to speak with.\n\nThe policy cannot be changed for #v 12#! months. Changing policy resets reform progress.

before: Foreign envoys now deal directly with our government. Defence and overseas affairs, once conducted through an overlord, rest on institutions of our own.\n\nThe merchants and local leaders who supported independence have not retired from public life. They have brought new petitions, expecting the government to honour its promises.
after: Foreign envoys now come straight to our government. The defence and overseas affairs we once handled through an overlord now run on rules of our own.\n\nThe merchants and local men who backed independence have not gone home. They are at our door with new petitions, asking the government to keep its old promises.

before: New arrangements for appointing officials are in place, and the laws have changed how power is distributed. Families accustomed to holding local office by birth must now contend with positions and powers defined by the state. Officials, soldiers and merchants who took part in reform are finding their places within these arrangements, which now guide the conduct of public affairs.
after: The new rules for appointing officials have taken hold, and the laws have redrawn how much power each class holds. Those who once ran their districts by right of birth must now work within posts and powers set by the government. The officials, soldiers and merchants who carried the reform are finding their places in the new order.

before: Aid from the mainland court helped the Toyotomi subdue Japan, binding tribute and maritime trade to the politics of the islands. Greater autonomy touches an overlord’s revenue, naval interests and influence in Japan. Those interests endure even when the old obligations are dissolved.
after: Troops from the mainland court helped the Toyotomi subdue Japan, and ever since, tribute and sea trade have been tangled up with the politics of the islands. Every measure of autonomy we win costs the overlord a measure of revenue, naval security and control over Japan. Those interests will not vanish just because the old treaty is dissolved.

before: Seek development funds from the northern government, offering closer commercial ties as a reason to support our growing industries.\n\nAfter receiving assistance, further funding is unavailable for #v 3#! years.
after: Use the promise of commercial cooperation as our opening, and ask the northern government to fund factories in Japan.\n\nAfter receiving assistance, further funding is unavailable for #v 3#! years.

before: Approach Dongzhou for funds to build workshops, making the case for closer trade and industrial development.\n\nAfter receiving assistance, further funding is unavailable for #v 3#! years.
after: On the strength of trade and industry, ask Dongzhou for money to build workshops.\n\nAfter receiving assistance, further funding is unavailable for #v 3#! years.

before: The southern government has long-standing commercial ties with Japan. Draw on these connections to seek funds for workshops and the training of skilled labour.\n\nAfter receiving assistance, further funding is unavailable for #v 3#! years.
after: The southern government has traded with Japan for many years. Follow those old connections and ask for a grant: capital for our workshops, and craftsmen to train our own.\n\nAfter receiving assistance, further funding is unavailable for #v 3#! years.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('jp_sender').GetNameNoFormatting] seeks greater authority over its own affairs and asks us to relax the present subject relationship. The envoy argues that greater autonomy would let the local government respond to domestic needs while preserving ties between our countries.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('jp_sender').GetNameNoFormatting] wants a larger hand in its own affairs and asks us to loosen the terms of its subordination. Its envoy says that with more autonomy they would not need to wait on our approval for every domestic matter, while the ties between our countries would stay as they are.

before: An envoy from [SCOPE.sCountry('jp_sender').GetNameNoFormatting] asks us to end the subject relationship. Their government seeks control over diplomacy, the military and trade, and wishes to deal with us as an independent country. We must decide whether to relinquish our authority as overlord.
after: An envoy from [SCOPE.sCountry('jp_sender').GetNameNoFormatting] demands an end to the subject relationship. From now on they would run their own diplomacy, army and trade, and deal with us as an independent country.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('jp_sender').GetNameNoFormatting] is seeking funds for workshop construction. Its envoy asks us for a grant to expand production and train skilled workers, arguing that growing industry would deepen ties between our countries.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('jp_sender').GetNameNoFormatting] is raising money to build workshops. Its envoy asks us for a grant to help expand production and train skilled workers.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('jp_sender').GetNameNoFormatting] proposes a settlement over southern Korea. Its government offers to relinquish claims to Busan and Yangho and transfer any territory it still holds there to Korea. The envoy asks us to accept these terms and settle the dispute.

before: The court has settled new arrangements for representation and public office. after: A new law has fixed the rules for deliberation and appointment. The old retainers still stand beside the monarch, but a different kind of official, versed in practical affairs, has begun to fill the provincial offices.\n\nReformers loyal to the dynasty believe these concessions will let the monarchy endure. Whether those who have won a voice will rest content with it, no one can say.

before: Those entitled to vote now choose their representatives, and newspapers can debate the conduct of government. after: Those entitled to vote now choose their representatives, and newspapers can debate the conduct of government. Officials face new rules of appointment, while political argument has spread beyond the old ruling families.\n\nThe new schools keep bringing more people into this world.

before: Edo now governs extensive northern territories. Garrisons can hold the roads, but they cannot conduct every part of provincial administration. The government needs officials to organise its revenue and spending, while the castle towns must accommodate merchants, craftsmen and people seeking work away from home. A country capable of sustaining ordinary government will be better placed to seek greater powers.
after: Edo now rules wide lands in the north. Its garrisons can hold the roads, but they cannot run the provinces. The government must hire officials and bring revenue and spending into a single ledger, and the castle towns must make room for merchants, craftsmen and people come from afar to find work. Only when these places can carry the daily business of government will Edo have its hands free to seek greater powers.

before: The courtiers of Kyoto and the merchants of Osaka have different connections and interests. Courtly rank does not pay soldiers, and private wealth does not become public revenue of its own accord. Officials must organise taxation and administration in the territories they govern so that the towns can sustain the new government.
after: The courtiers of Kyoto and the merchants of Osaka each have their own circles and their own calculations. Court titles do not pay soldiers, and merchants' money does not flow into the treasury of its own accord. The officials in charge of revenue must put the income and business of the present territories in order, so that the two cities can support the new government.

before: Partition has deprived the Toyotomi retainers of their former authority over Japan, but the troops and households remaining in the west still need support. Old prestige cannot settle who collects the revenue or conducts local government. A dependable administration must be established in the surviving territories, with castle towns serving as centres of government, taxation and employment.
after: Since the partition, the Toyotomi can no longer command all of Japan. Yet not one of the soldiers and retainers in the western provinces has gone, and all of them wait for their rice stipends. Old prestige alone can no longer decide where the annual tax is collected or who governs the villages. The Toyotomi regime must set up reliable magistrates' offices in the lands it still holds, and make the castle towns into places for collecting taxes, doing government business and hiring labour.

before: Our overlord has agreed to loosen its control, granting us a more autonomous status. The two governments have established a five-year truce.
after: Our overlord has agreed to loosen its hold, raising us one step towards autonomy. The two governments have agreed a five-year truce. Matters that once needed permission at every turn can now be taken in hand ourselves.

after: [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_a2_khanate').GetName] has been established. Indigenous settlers from Dongzhou and the United States have brought their families, possessions and hopes of keeping their land to the new country. before: The restoration of the house of Moctezuma and the Andean court has won support among Indigenous villages. The republics promised liberty, yet their new rulers still encroach on common land and exact taxes. For those who work the fields, a change of flag in the capital has done little to lighten their burden.\n\nSupporters of the old dynasties are turning this resentment to their advantage. They promise to protect common land and local rights in return for the villages' people and arms. Rural communities, in turn, hope to use a monarch's prestige to resist the depredations of the new elite. The government must decide whether to recognise the dynasty, draw away its supporters through local councils and land reform, or send the army to silence the calls for restoration.
after: The restoration of the house of Moctezuma and the Andean court has won support among Indigenous villages. They promise to protect common land and local rights in return for the villages' people and arms. Rural communities, in turn, hope to use a monarch's prestige to resist the depredations of the new elite.

before: The restorationists have formed a separate government, bringing village militias together under the old dynasty's name to claim rule over the whole country. The former government refuses to surrender the territory that has broken away. War will now decide who protects the common lands, who collects the taxes and whose orders the army obeys.\n\nBoth sides intend to annex their opponent and refuse a peace that leaves the country divided. The victorious government will also have to answer the political demands of those who fought in its cause.
after: The restorationists have formed a separate government, bringing village militias together under the old dynasty's name to claim rule over the whole country. The former government refuses to surrender the territory that has broken away. War will now decide who protects the common lands, who collects the taxes and whose orders the army obeys.\n\nBoth sides mean to annex the other and refuse any peace that leaves the country divided.

before: The army has dispersed restorationist gatherings and disrupted contacts among local leaders. Advocates of force applaud the government for asserting its authority at last. The Indigenous people facing searches and arrests have further cause to believe that this government protects only those who seize their land.\n\nThe restoration movement has lost ground for the moment, but resentment in the countryside has deepened. Supporters of the old dynasty who escaped the soldiers are unlikely to let such an opportunity pass.
after: The army has broken up the restorationist meetings and cut the lines between local leaders. Those who wanted force are cheering; the Indigenous people hunted down in the searches are more certain than ever that this government protects only the men who took their land.\n\nThe movement has been beaten down for now, but the countryside's resentment runs deeper. The dynasty's supporters who escaped the soldiers will hardly let such an opportunity slip.

before: The army has acted. The countryside may yet refuse to submit.
after: Anyone else who gathers a crowd will get the same.

before: The opposing government has lost its last territory, and the country is reunited. The army is taking control of the provinces. Taxes collected by rival authorities during the war will once again be sent to a single capital.\n\nMany in the countryside supported the defeated side. The lowering of its flag will hardly change their convictions. The government must decide how to treat these people and the demands for which they took up arms.
after: The opposing government has lost its last territory, and the country is reunited. The army is taking control of the provinces. Taxes collected by rival authorities during the war will once again be sent to a single capital.\n\nMany in the countryside followed the losing side. Its flag has come down, but their convictions have not come down with it.

before: Changes in territory and government have interrupted the restoration struggle. Our former rival can no longer continue the fight, yet we have not taken possession of all its lands.\n\nThe government must reassess its friends and enemies in these altered circumstances. Unresolved local questions will have to be addressed within the new borders.
after: Changes in territory and government have cut the restoration struggle short. Our rival can no longer fight on, yet we have not taken all of its lands.\n\nWe must work out anew who is friend and who is foe, and settle the unfinished local questions within the new borders.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_restoration_applicant').GetName] proposes that both countries recognise the existing Inca court and that its territory be joined to ours. after: [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_restoration_applicant').GetName] proposes that both countries recognise the existing Inca court and that its territory be joined to ours. before: The American Civil War has shaken authority on the Great Plains, while Dongzhou's new registration law has brought Indigenous grievances to the fore. Community leaders are renewing ties with supporters of the earlier uprising, hoping to use the upheaval in both countries to establish a khanate of their own.\n\nLand holds this alliance together. Migration and registration determine where people may live and who decides their status. To win the communities' support, a new khan must promise to defend these rights and possess the strength to resist intervention by both powers.
after: The American Civil War has shaken authority on the Great Plains, while Dongzhou's new registration law has brought Indigenous grievances to the fore. Community leaders are renewing ties with supporters of the earlier uprising, hoping to use the upheaval in both countries to establish a khanate of their own.\n\nThis alliance is rooted in land. Where people move and how they are registered decide where they can survive. To win the communities' loyalty, a new khan must first promise to defend these things, and then have the strength to keep both powers out.

before: The United States and Dongzhou both demand the khanate's annexation. Indigenous people who have only just settled on the Plains must take up arms again to defend the homes they struggled to obtain. Having acclaimed a common khan, the communities expect him to unite their scattered forces against the two invaders.\n\nThe new khan needs their recruits and supplies, while local leaders insist on retaining their rights. War has brought these peoples together. Whether their union can hold will determine whether they can remain on these plains.
after: The United States and Dongzhou both demand the khanate's annexation. Indigenous people who have only just settled on the Plains must take up arms again to defend the homes they struggled to obtain. Having acclaimed a common khan, the communities expect him to unite their scattered forces against the two invaders.\n\nThe new khan needs their men and their grain; the local leaders want to keep their own rights. War has knotted the peoples together, and if the knot comes loose, they will have to leave these plains.

before: Territorial cession and migration on the Great Plains have changed the balance of power in North America. With the support of Indigenous communities, the khanate has established a government and seeks to bind settlers, land and local militias into a new state. The longer we allow it to take root, the harder our territorial claims will be to uphold.\n\nOur government intends to end the khanate's rule through annexation. The new khan hopes to force the intervening powers to submit and win prestige for the Plains Compact. At stake are both the territory itself and the right to determine the lives of its Indigenous inhabitants.
after: Since the Great Plains were ceded, migrating peoples have poured onto the grasslands. With the backing of Indigenous communities, the khanate has set up a government and means to twist settlers, land and local militias into a single state. Let it put down roots, and our claim to this land will grow weaker by the year.\n\nWe will annex the khanate. The new khan, for his part, hopes to drive off the interveners and use a victory to stamp the Plains Compact's authority on every band.

before: Both interventions have ended, and the khanate has preserved its government. The communities joined forces to resist outside powers, and those who migrated here can now remain and build their lives on the Plains.\n\nThe new khan must reach agreement with local leaders on taxation, defence and authority. Disagreements set aside while they fought together will return in the course of everyday government. The Plains Compact will endure only so long as the state serves the interests of those who sustain it.
after: Both interventions are over, and the khanate has kept its government. The communities stood together against outside powers, and the settlers have finally made a home on the Plains.\n\nNow the new khan must talk taxes, defence and power with the local leaders. The quarrels shelved in wartime are being laid back on the table, one by one.

before: From the northern plains to the southern mountains, the Americas now answer to one government. The former state of Dongzhou is gone. The new [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] has inherited its name, abolished the old social hierarchy and assumed rule over the continent as a republic.\n\nIndigenous peoples who once petitioned for land, status and local rights have become the masters of this country. This vast republic is now their responsibility. They must decide how common laws will enter the lives of its many communities, and whose interests their newly acquired power will protect.
after: From the northern plains to the southern mountains, the Americas now answer to one government. The former state of Dongzhou is gone. The new [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] has inherited its name, abolished the old social hierarchy and assumed rule over the continent as a republic.\n\nIndigenous peoples who once ran from office to office for land, status and local rights are now the masters of this country. A republic this large is theirs to carry from now on.

before: With registration complete, Manchu and Mongol communities left in the second tier have begun to leave the republic. Some have gone to [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_a2_cne_country').GetName], others to the west of [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_a2_usa_country').GetName], carrying their families and old ties to new lands.\n\nEach community has a seventy percent chance of choosing the former destination and thirty percent of choosing the latter. Along with their people and possessions, the republic is losing the hopes they once held of an equal place within it.
after: With registration complete, Manchu and Mongol communities left in the second tier have begun to leave the republic. Some have gone to [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_a2_cne_country').GetName], others to the west of [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_a2_usa_country').GetName], carrying their families and old ties to new lands.\n\nEach community has a seventy percent chance of choosing the former destination and thirty percent of choosing the latter. In the end, the equal registration they waited for never came.

before: The allotted time has passed without the Inca court agreeing to union. A shared dynastic tradition has not brought the two governments under a single authority. Each remains responsible for its own people and territory.\n\nLocal communities must reconcile their hopes for the court with the politics of the present. Talks may be renewed, but an unanswered proposal cannot alter the fact that two states still stand.
after: The deadline has passed, and the Inca court never agreed to union. For all their shared dynastic tradition, the two governments still each rule their own land and people.\n\nTalks can be reopened later. For now, the two states stand apart as before.

before: The Inca court has refused the proposal for union. A common dynastic tradition may draw the two sides closer, but it has not persuaded their present rulers to accept a single state.\n\nOur government must continue to address land and local politics at home, rather than entrust these responsibilities to a reply from the court. Talks may be renewed once the waiting period has ended.
after: The Inca court has turned down the union. The two houses share a dynastic tradition and can call each other kin, but neither will give up its throne or its court.\n\nVillage land and local quarrels are still ours to deal with; we cannot wait on an answer from the court. Once the waiting period has ended, we may send envoys again.

before: The dynasty's supporters have summoned local communities anew to discuss the political arrangements between court and countryside. The cause of restoration is established, but local leaders still want to know what place their lands and representatives will have under its rule.\n\nThe country must live with the divisions left by earlier struggles. The court needs rural support, and the countryside demands protection for its interests. Their compact will have reason to endure only when these claims take effect in everyday government.
after: The dynasty's supporters have called the local communities together again to settle the terms between court and countryside. The restoration's legitimacy is established, but local leaders still want to know exactly where their land and their representatives stand under the new rule.\n\nThe court needs the villages behind it, and the villages need the court to protect them. This compact must be honoured in every tax and every levy of troops.

before: Both intervening governments have been forced to accept humiliation, and the khanate has preserved its government. The victory of the Army of the Plains Compact has brought prestige to the union between the new khan and the communities. Settlers can remain in their new homes.\n\nWar united them against outside powers. They must now agree on taxation, the burdens of defence and the rights retained by each community. The Plains Compact will need more than past victories to become a lasting government.
after: Both intervening governments have been forced to accept humiliation, and the khanate has preserved its government. The victory of the Army of the Plains Compact has brought prestige to the union between the new khan and the communities. Settlers can remain in their new homes.\n\nNow that the fighting is over, they must agree on how to raise taxes, how to share the burden of defence and which rights stay with each community. Battles already won will not hold up a lasting government.

before: One intervention ended in the opponent's humiliation, and the other has also come to a close. The khanate has preserved its government and territory. Those who settled here can remain and earn their living on the Plains.\n\nThe communities gathered beneath the new khan's banner to resist invasion. They must now discuss taxation, defence and local authority. In peacetime, those who shared the burdens of war will need to see what the common undertaking offers them in return.
after: One intervention ended in the opponent's humiliation, and the other has also come to a close. The khanate has preserved its government and territory. Those who settled here can remain and earn their living on the Plains.\n\nThe communities gathered under the new khan's banner to hold off invasion; now the talk is of taxes, defence and local power. In war, everyone shouldered the load together; in peace, each will want to see what share comes to him.

before: Both interventions have ended. The khanate forced neither opponent to accept humiliation, but it has preserved its government. The communities of the Plains can continue to build their new homes.\n\nThe new khan still depends on local leaders and settlers for support. How taxes and defence are shared, and how local rights are protected, will determine how long this compact for survival can endure.
after: Both interventions have ended. The khanate forced neither opponent to accept humiliation, but it has preserved its government. The communities of the Plains can continue to build their new homes.\n\nThe new khan still leans on the local leaders and the settlers. How taxes and defence are shared out, and how each district's rights are kept: on these few things hangs a compact made to survive.

after: [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_khanate_opponent').GetName] has withdrawn from treaties with the khanate containing an alliance or defensive pact, clearing the way for intervention.
