before: Supporters of the old dynasty have established ties with Indigenous villages. Local leaders are gathering recruits and supplies, hoping a new government will protect their lands and autonomy. The restorationists intend to use this rural strength to restore the dynasty's rule.\n\nPreparations will last twelve months. The government of [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] can still seek cooperation through negotiations over local councils and land rights, but delay gives the restorationists more time to organise. The response of the villages will determine the strength these networks can summon to arms.
after: Supporters of the old dynasty have established ties with Indigenous villages. Local leaders are gathering recruits and supplies, hoping a new government will protect their lands and autonomy. The restorationists intend to use this rural strength to restore the dynasty's rule.\n\nThe preparations will take twelve months. The government of [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] can still win over the villages with talks on local councils and land rights; the longer it waits, the better organised the restorationists become.

before: Conquest has brought peoples of different faiths, languages and histories under Ottoman rule. Officials in Anatolia, provincial interests in the Balkans and newly incorporated communities all expect the government to protect their interests.\n\nSchools, effective administration and a secure livelihood can strengthen allegiance to the state. Prolonged war and discrimination deepen divisions. Lasting rule requires cooperation in the provinces as well as success in conquest.
after: Conquest has brought peoples of every faith, language and history into the Ottoman realm. Officials in Anatolia, local powers in the Balkans and newly incorporated peoples all expect Istanbul to protect their interests.\n\nSchools, government offices and a secure living can make the provinces accept the state; endless war and discrimination only drive people further away. Conquered lands are held only if the provinces are willing to cooperate.

before: The central government and the provinces continue to cooperate, though allegiance to the state remains uncertain.
after: The centre and the provinces still cooperate, but the peoples' attachment to the state is not yet firm.

before: The Near Western War exposed the weaknesses of the old army. With Western Qin driven out of central China, officers in Istanbul urge an advance eastward to restore Ottoman standing in the Islamic world.\n\nThe achievements and failures of the Tanzimat will shape this army. The government must raise the money and decide how much strength to devote to territorial demands and how much to military reform.
after: The Near Western War laid bare the faults of the old army. With Western Qin driven out of central China, officers in Istanbul urge an advance eastward to restore Ottoman standing in the Islamic world.\n\nWhatever the Tanzimat achieved, and whatever walls it ran into, will tell on this army. The money must be raised, and both the new territorial demands and the army's reform are waiting for it.

before: The struggle is not over.
after: The West has not been won over yet.

before: The Tang-Persian court knows both the military government of Qin and the merchants and great families of Persia. The Near-Western War brought land and prestige, but left the Empire's future course unsettled. The court may seek Ili's help for expansion to the west, or exploit unrest in Western Qin to pursue conquests of its own.
after: The rulers of the Tang-Persian court know the military government of Qin as well as they know Persia's merchants and great families. The Near-Western War brought them land and prestige, but the empire's direction is still undecided: push west with Ili's help, or use Western Qin's local troubles to strike east on its own account?

before: The offices introduced by the military government stand alongside local academies, religious schools and family networks. To make officials of these different backgrounds work together, the court needs reliable appointments and schools capable of training their successors.
after: The offices brought in by the military government stand alongside local academies, religious schools and families. Getting officials of such different backgrounds to work under one roof needs reliable rules for appointment, and schools to train new men.

before: Cotton fields, weavers and travelling merchants sustain Persia's prosperity. By linking the countryside to its towns with railways, the court hopes to make the lands won in the Near-Western War support new workshops as well as the army.
after: Cotton fields, weavers and passing caravans keep Persia prosperous. The court wants railways to join farms to towns, so that the lands won in the Near-Western War feed new workshops as well as the army.

before: The craftsmen who accompanied the mission have arrived in our workshops. They are teaching surveying, construction and machine maintenance. Local workers and merchants must now turn those skills into lasting enterprises.
after: The craftsmen who came with the mission are now at work in our workshops, teaching surveying, building and the repair of machines. Whether these skills become lasting industries is up to our own workers and merchants.

before: The court has formally asserted its claim to [SCOPE.sStateRegion('nesnd_per_claim_region').GetName]. Commanders and merchants can prepare their next moves. Possession of the territory must still be secured through diplomacy or war.
after: The court has formally asserted its claim to [SCOPE.sStateRegion('nesnd_per_claim_region').GetName]. The note has been delivered; who actually holds the land will still be settled by diplomacy or the sword.

before: A foreign power has opposed our claim to [SCOPE.sStateRegion('nesnd_per_claim_region').GetName]. The court has failed to secure recognition. It must improve its diplomatic position before renewing the demand.
after: Our note on [SCOPE.sStateRegion('nesnd_per_claim_region').GetName] has been blocked by a great power. To win that recognition, we must first change the diplomatic situation there.

before: The government has chosen expansion to the west, but the proposed tributary arrangement with Ili has not taken effect. Commanders and merchants can still pursue a western policy, drawing on the troops, revenues and support presently available.
after: The court has settled on expansion westward, but the planned tributary pact with Ili has fallen through. The west can still be pursued; the troops and the money will simply have to be found by ourselves.

before: The army needs pay, towns need roads, and schools and new laws compete for the court's support. Prestige won in the Near Western War cannot provide all of them. Relations with Ili may bring assistance, but lasting authority must also rest on our own schools, industry and public order.
after: The army wants pay, the towns want roads, and the schools and new laws are waiting for money too. The lingering glory of the Near Western War will not get any of it done. Ili can lend a hand, but whether the court stands firm depends in the end on our own schools, trade and peace at home.

before: We cannot authorize this expense.
after: Not this expense. Not now.

before: The central government has approved garrison funding of #v £8,000#! a week for one year. Reduced tribute is also included in the proposal. The garrison and Luzon squadron would retain their existing deployment, without joining the court’s main force.\n\nThe Pacification Commission has won an opportunity to share the expense, but Luzon must still maintain the troops and ships. Once we sign, it will fall to us to decide how this money should serve both military pay and civilian livelihoods.
after: The central government has approved garrison funding of #v £8,000#! a week for one year, and reduced tribute has been written into the proposal. The garrison and the Luzon squadron keep their present deployment and need not join the court's main force.\n\nThe money has been won, but Luzon must still feed its own troops and ships. Once we sign, how this money is divided between soldiers' pay and the people's livelihood is our own affair.

before: The central government has agreed to the proposed division of naval duties. Under this arrangement, the ships of the line belong to the court’s main force, while the frigates and the Western Administration’s garrison remain in Luzon. The centre bears the upkeep of the ocean-going warships, allowing the Pacification Commission to concentrate on the islands’ garrison and coastal defence.\n\nThe proposal covers the transfer of ships, reduced tribute and exemption from service, with #v £3,000#! a week in subsidies for the first year. Once transferred, the warships remain under central control. Luzon may negotiate further funding if difficulties persist. The agreement before us still awaits the Commission’s final signature.
after: The central government has agreed to the proposed division of naval duties. Under this arrangement, the ships of the line belong to the court's main force, while the frigates and the Western Administration's garrison remain in Luzon. The centre bears the upkeep of the ocean-going warships, allowing the Pacification Commission to concentrate on the islands' garrison and coastal defence.\n\nThe transfer of ships, reduced tribute and exemption from service are all in the proposal, with #v £3,000#! a week in subsidies for the first year. Once the warships are handed over, they belong to central command; if Luzon still struggles, it may ask for more funds. All that remains is for the Commission to sign.

before: After negotiations, the two countries have amended the military funding treaty. The payments and obligations previously agreed will now follow the new terms.\n\nThe Pacification Commission must rearrange its expenditure accordingly. When payments are due, and who bears which responsibilities, will determine how much remains for soldiers’ pay and local revenues. We should read the new treaty closely before making plans.
after: After several rounds of talks, the two countries have revised the military funding treaty. The payments and duties agreed before now follow the new terms.\n\nThe Pacification Commission must rework its spending under the new treaty: when the money arrives, which duties belong to whom, and how much is left for soldiers' pay and the districts, it is all written there.

before: Luzon asks the central government to share the annual cost of its garrison and naval defence. The Pacification Commission is willing to remit tribute as before. It argues, however, that troops and ships awaiting the court’s summons should receive part of their support from the central treasury.\n\nThe proposal requests #v £8,700#! a week for one year. The court’s ocean-going forces and Luzon’s local livelihoods both draw upon the islands’ revenues. If the districts must bear the whole expense, they will have ever less room to restore production.
after: Luzon asks the central government to share the annual cost of its garrison and naval defence. The Pacification Commission is willing to remit tribute as before. It argues, however, that troops and ships awaiting the court's summons should receive part of their support from the central treasury.\n\nThe proposal requests #v £8,700#! a week for one year. The court's ocean-going forces and Luzon's own livelihood both eat from the same bowl: the islands' revenue. Leave the whole burden on the districts, and they will have nothing left to rebuild production.

before: The central government has approved a subsidy of #v £8,700#! a week for one year. Tribute will be remitted as before, and the Pacification Commission will continue to maintain the fleet and garrison, with the court meeting part of the expense from its treasury.\n\nThe payments still await Luzon’s final signature. This contribution can ease our immediate difficulties, but it cannot administer the islands for us. Providing for the soldiers in camp while allowing local livelihoods to recover remains the Commission’s responsibility.
after: The central government has approved a subsidy of #v £8,700#! a week for one year. Tribute is remitted as before, the Pacification Commission still maintains the fleet and garrison, and the court covers part of the cost from its treasury.\n\nThe payments await only Luzon's signature. The subsidy will ease the immediate strain; the islands' affairs remain the Commission's to manage.

before: The central government has accepted the proposal to divide naval responsibilities. Under its terms, twenty ships of the line belong to central command, while frigates and garrison troops remain to defend the islands. The upkeep of the transferred warships falls to the centre.\n\nThe Pacification Commission will receive #v £3,700#! a week for one year. Tribute and exemption from service follow their respective terms. With military duties apportioned, the revenues retained must sustain Luzon’s own livelihoods. This agreement still awaits our final signature.
after: The central government has accepted the proposal to divide naval responsibilities. Under its terms, twenty ships of the line belong to central command, while frigates and garrison troops remain to defend the islands. The upkeep of the transferred warships falls to the centre.\n\nThe Pacification Commission will receive #v £3,700#! a week for one year; tribute and exemption from service follow their own terms. With the military duties divided, the money saved can go to Luzon's own livelihood. The agreement awaits only our signature.

before: We have squandered too many years.
after: Ten years, wasted just like that.

before: Trade routes, village communities and military colonies brought peoples of many origins under the Chen emperors of Qin. The Western Regions Han-Qiang emerged from that expansion and now provide much of the country’s manpower and revenue. Prosperity encourages a common identity. Conscription and hardship can lead people back to older loyalties of kinship, faith and homeland.
after: Trade routes, villages and military colonies drew people of many origins under the rule of the Chen emperors of Qin. The Western Regions Han-Qiang are a product of the empire's expansion, and the empire's soldiers and revenue come from them. In good years, people are glad to share a common identity; when conscription grows heavy and times turn hard, the old clan names, faiths and home villages are dug up again.

before: Petitions no longer satisfy the associations of the frontier. They are gathering provisions, approaching old noble families and religious leaders, and challenging imperial tax collectors and recruiting officers in the name of local peoples. Ili may yet recover their allegiance. Delay will allow scattered resistance to grow into a common revolt.
after: Petitions no longer satisfy the associations of the frontier. They are gathering provisions, approaching old noble families and religious leaders, and challenging imperial tax collectors and recruiting officers in the name of local peoples. Ili still has time to win back their loyalty; wait any longer, and the scattered revolts will join into one.

before: The Chen imperial house has not forgotten the passes of Hexi or the fields of Guanzhong. By recovering the roads to the east and rebuilding its army and administration, the Empire could make these ancestral lands the foundation of a renewed struggle for China.
after: The Chen imperial house cannot forget the passes of Hexi and the fields of Guanzhong. Win back the roads to the east, rebuild the army and the administration, and Ili can set out from the ancestral lands to contend for China once more.

before: Qin forces once again control the roads through Hexi and Guanzhong. The court must decide how to use its victory: prepare fresh armies for the march east, or first establish new institutions, industries and a common identity throughout the recovered provinces.
after: Qin forces have retaken the roads through Hexi and Guanzhong. The ancestral lands are ours again; how should this victory be used? March east with the new armies, or first let the new offices, industries and common identity take root in every province?

before: The Hungarian question has reached a settlement, but debate across the country continues. Scholars in Prague seek support for their schools, while officials in Vienna want provincial administrations capable of carrying out common policies. New investment will help determine how the central government holds together provinces with different languages and interests.
after: The Hungarian question has been settled for now, but the arguing has not stopped. The scholars of Prague want schools of their own; the officials of Vienna want the provinces to carry out common policy to the letter. Provinces with different languages and interests still have to be held together, and Vienna must find a way to do it.

before: The Tanzimat has left laws and unfulfilled ambitions. Coastal merchants want to move their goods; provincial officials complain of inadequate revenues. If the country is to escape its dependence on debt and the costs of war, its ports and administration must sustain more than promises of reform.
after: The Tanzimat has left laws and unfulfilled ambitions. Coastal merchants want to move their goods; provincial officials complain of inadequate revenues. If the country is ever to stop worrying about foreign debt and war indemnities, its ports, trade routes and provincial offices must actually work.

before: Cotton travels down the Nile to the coast, while imported cloth makes the return journey. The army and government tax this commerce, but Egyptian craftsmen want workshops of their own. The development of schools, textiles and ports will shape Egypt's room for manoeuvre among its neighbours and foreign powers.
after: Cotton travels down the Nile to the coast, and foreign cloth comes back up from the ports. The army and the court tax this trade, but Egypt's craftsmen want workshops of their own. Build up schools, textiles and ports together, and Egypt will face the powers around it with a little more confidence.

before: Trains from Silesia bring coal and iron to Berlin, along with new petitions. Railway companies seek support for freight services, while manufacturers want to expand the production of machinery and tools. The officers favour more transport capacity, though they have drawn up their own calculations for its use. The government must decide where further support will go.
after: Trains from Silesia bring coal and iron to Berlin, along with new petitions. The railway companies want the government to back trunk-line freight; the manufacturers want to build more machines and tools. The officers naturally favour more carrying capacity, though they have worked out a separate military use for every station.

before: Provincial schools are training a new generation of teachers and officials. Some want them to serve their own communities. Others would bring them into Vienna's administration. Both claim to be strengthening the country. Their disagreement concerns where education and authority should take root.
after: Provincial schools are beginning to turn out a new generation of teachers and clerks. Some want them kept at home; others want them drawn into Vienna's bureaucracy. Both sides say they are serving the country. At bottom, the question is whether the money for education stays in the provinces, or the people who do the work go to the centre.

before: Shipping records and tax accounts are beginning to show the results of recent investment. Merchants ask that support remain with the ports, while treasury officials see an opportunity to strengthen administration. The government cannot rely indefinitely on extraordinary levies. Further investment calls for a choice.
after: The port's shipping returns and the tax office's ledgers are starting to show what the investment has achieved. Merchants ask the government to keep its money in shipping; treasury officials say this is the moment to put the administration in order. Emergency levies are no way to run a country for long.

before: Egyptian workshops can now turn more of the country's cotton into cloth. Manufacturers seek help to expand. Teachers warn the government that an industry cannot prosper for long if literacy and technical knowledge remain the preserve of a few. The first gains of prosperity have brought another decision.
after: Egypt's workshops can now weave more of the country's cotton into cloth. The manufacturers want to expand production, but the schoolteachers warn the court that if reading and skills stay in the hands of a few, the new industries will soon run short of hands again.

before: Schools, ports and workshops have begun to show results. State representatives demand continued investment in the provinces, while the government in the capital hopes to use these achievements to strengthen its authority. The next allocation of funds will determine which receives support first.
after: The provincial schools, ports and workshops have all shown results. The state representatives want to keep the money flowing to the provinces; the government in the capital wants to use these achievements to shore up its authority.

before: Schools and transport in the South are beginning to show new life. Freed people seek wider access to education, while business interests press for continued railway support. Emancipation was a beginning. Further investment will shape the place of the newly free in the economy that follows.
after: Schools and transport in the South are showing some signs of life. Those who broke free of bondage want the chance to learn, and the business interests are urging the Union to keep supporting the railways. Abolishing slavery was only the beginning.

before: Railways have linked some mining districts to the coast, and Lima's merchants are discussing larger investments. Mine owners want to expand production. Engineers fear that a shortage of skilled people will leave new machinery idle. The government can support further output or invest in the knowledge needed to sustain it.
after: Railways now link part of the mining country to the coast, and Lima's merchants have begun to talk of bigger investments. The mine owners want to expand while the going is good; the engineers worry that without enough skilled men, the new machinery will simply stand idle.

before: The promised programme of improvements has not been completed. Schools, industry and transport remain pressing concerns, but the expectations surrounding this undertaking have faded. What has been built will remain in use. What was promised will not be so easily forgotten.
after: This round of improvements was never finished as hoped. Schools, industry and transport are as pressing as ever, but the hopes that gathered around the programme have melted away. What was built still stands, and the promises that were broken are still remembered.

before: Indigenous communities seek control over their land and a voice for local representatives. The central government insists on its authority over the provinces. Whether local councils can offer a compromise, or the dispute leads to independence and war, will shape the region’s future.
after: Indigenous communities want their land in their own hands, and their own representatives running village affairs. The central government will not give up an inch of its authority. If the local councils can reach terms, all may yet live in peace; if not, it will mean independence and war.

before: Indigenous communities have established a separate government and now contest the former government’s authority. Land, military allegiance and the political standing of local communities are at stake. Annexing the opposing country would end their divided rule.
after: Indigenous communities have set up a separate government and are contesting the old government's right to rule. Who owns the land, whom the army obeys and what standing the communities will have are all staked on this struggle. Only when one side annexes the other will the divided rule end.

before: War has begun between the Indigenous polity and the former government, with each demanding the other’s annexation. Land, armed forces and the political standing of local communities are at stake.
after: War has broken out between the Indigenous polity and the former government, and each demands the other's annexation.

before: Prepare for the confrontation.
after: To arms.

before: The army has dispersed gatherings and disrupted contact between local leaders. The Armed Forces support the use of force, but resentment has deepened in the countryside. Disputes over land and local power remain unsettled.
after: The army has broken up the gatherings and scattered the leaders' networks. The Armed Forces approve, but resentment in the countryside has grown deeper still. Not one of the disputes over land and power has been resolved.

before: The opposing government’s entire territory has been annexed by [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName]. Divided rule has ended, and local communities must now seek their place under the new government.
after: The opposing government's entire territory has been annexed by [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName]. Divided rule is over; the local communities must now fight for their standing all over again under the new government.

before: The dispute has ended without our country annexing its opponent. The government must still address local claims to land and political rights.
after: The dispute is over, and we failed to annex our opponent. The local communities' demands for land and rights are still there.

before: Face the situation as it stands.
after: We will take it one step at a time.

before: People displaced by the defeat of an Indigenous polity have arrived in [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName]. They bring family ties and the need to rebuild their livelihoods.
after: With the Indigenous polity fallen, people who fled their homes have arrived in [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName]. They bring their family ties with them, and demands that were never met.

before: The frontier garrisons have secured the roads onto the steppe. Russia must now decide how to govern the Kazakh districts under its authority and whether to press territorial claims farther south along the caravan routes.
after: The frontier garrisons have retaken the roads onto the steppe. How to govern the Kazakh districts now under Russia, and whether to press claims farther south along the caravan routes, are questions now before St Petersburg.

before: South of the steppe, the river roads connect the markets of Bukhara, Khiva and Fergana. Russian cavalry can ride those roads, but it cannot carry commerce past every customs post by force. The government must decide whether to seek the cooperation of the local authorities or press its demands with troops.
after: South of the steppe, the river roads connect the markets of Bukhara, Khiva and Fergana. Russian cavalry can ride those roads, but it cannot carry commerce past every customs post by force.

before: The government has permitted local organisations to operate, giving their movements more room to win support.
after: The government has allowed local organisations to operate, and the movements can now openly win supporters.

before: The police are suppressing local organisations and restricting their movements' public activities.
after: The police are suppressing local organisations, and the movements cannot act in the open.

before: Changes in the political situation or the country's circumstances have ended the previous arrangements.
after: The political situation or the country's circumstances have changed, and the old way of handling the matter has been dropped.

before: The former arrangements for public works and political cooperation in Italy have ended.
after: Public works and political cooperation in Italy have come to a close for now.

before: The former Dongzhou government's arrangements for local works and civic affairs have ended.
after: The local works and civic affairs run by the former Dongzhou government have been wound up.

before: The Southern Dynasty's previous deliberations on constitutional law, education and industry have ended.
after: The South's planned deliberations on the constitution, education and industry have come to nothing.

before: Changes in the country's status or territory have ended its former programme of local economic and public development.
after: The country's status or territory has changed, and the work on local livelihoods has come to a halt.

before: The sea between Australia and New Zealand has become a common trading route for their producers. Ports can hire workers and local industries have found outlets for their goods, giving the Far South more than a single centre of production on which to depend.\n\nFarmers and labourers have firmer livelihoods, and the government can draw revenue from their work. The schools and local services it hopes to maintain will depend on the goods crossing these waters, and on the people who produce them.
after: More and more cargo ships are crossing the sea between Australia and New Zealand. The ports can afford to hire dockhands, the interior has found buyers for its produce, and the Far South no longer lives off a single source of wealth.\n\nFarmers and labourers have a surer living, and the government's revenue has grown with it. The schools and local services of the years ahead will depend on the goods carried over this sea, and on the people who produce them.

before: Viable industries have taken root in the upper country around $STATE_MANDALAY$ and the lower reaches at $STATE_PEGU$. Transport carries their produce to market, providing farmers, labourers and merchants with a steadier living.\n\nThese links between the upper and lower country give the government the means to attend to local affairs. With revenue to support them, administration and education can become more than aspirations. The division of that revenue will help determine how much each region gains from this growth.
after: Upriver at $STATE_MANDALAY$ and downriver at $STATE_PEGU$, industries have found their feet. Transport carries the produce of both to market, and farmers, labourers and merchants all have money coming in.\n\nNow that taxes have somewhere to come from, offices and schools are more than talk. But how that money is shared out, upriver and downriver each have their own reckoning.

before: More dependable market links now connect production in Bangkok and the provinces. The centres of population and wealth need goods from elsewhere, while provincial producers need customers if they are to pay wages and taxes.\n\nThese ties bring the government more revenue, along with competing demands on its use. The army needs supplies, and the provinces need schools and public services. Those whose work fills the treasury will expect the state to take an interest in their lives.
after: Trade between Bangkok and the outer provinces has settled into a steady course. The crowded, wealthy capital needs what the provinces produce; the provincial workshops and estates, with a market at last, can pay wages and pay their taxes.\n\nOnce money reached the treasury, the hands held out for it soon followed: the army wants its pay, and the provinces want schools and funds for public business. Those who earned this revenue for the country now expect the country to do something for their lives in return.

before: Production and shipping between Australia and New Zealand can now support public affairs in both regions. Offices have staff and education has a firmer footing. The Far South is acquiring the revenue and trained people it needs to sustain its own affairs.\n\nThe government can speak with greater confidence abroad. Whoever sits across the negotiating table, the wealth created by these communities and the public institutions they maintain give substance to our claim to greater independence.
after: The production and shipping of Australia and New Zealand can now pay for public affairs in both. The offices are staffed and the schools are open; the Far South earns its own money and trains its own people.\n\nThe government stands a little straighter when it deals with foreign powers. The wealth these communities have built is the ground on which the Far South claims its independence.

before: Production, transport and public services have gained a more secure footing in the upper country and the lower reaches around $STATE_PEGU$. The government has revenue, and local people can undertake administration and teaching. Relations between the two regions now extend well beyond the exchange of goods.\n\nBurma can draw on these resources to conduct its own affairs. Foreign relations will still require care, but the country has more wealth and trained people on which to rely when faced with demands from abroad.
after: Production, transport and public business have found firm footing upriver and downriver at $STATE_PEGU$. The treasury has an income, local people are serving as officials and teachers, and the two halves of the country now exchange far more than goods.\n\nBurma can run its own affairs on these savings. When foreign powers make their next demand, the court will have both money and men behind it.

before: Production in Bangkok and the provinces can now sustain public services, with firmer foundations for administration, education and defence. Government revenue is becoming the means to uphold our autonomy.\n\nThis achievement will hardly end disagreement. The provinces want schools and improvements, the army requires dependable supplies, and the central government has expenses of its own. The argument now concerns what kind of country this revenue should sustain as much as where the money is to come from.
after: Production in Bangkok and the outer provinces can now pay for public business, and administration, schools and defence all have something to stand on. Little by little, the treasury's income is turning into the means for Siam to stand alone.\n\nMore money has brought more quarrels. The provinces want schools and public works, the army wants its pay on time, and the capital has bills of its own. The argument is no longer only about where the money comes from, but about what kind of Siam it should build.

before: A small country's freedom of action often rests on the livelihoods of ordinary people. Farmers must be able to pay their taxes, labourers to find work, and merchants to carry goods to willing buyers before the government can afford administration, education and defence. When producers are overwhelmed by rent, debt and unemployment, every grand undertaking makes another demand on people who can scarcely bear it.\n\nForeign capital can bring money and knowledge, and an overlord's support may ease some burdens. To have a stronger voice in these relationships, the country needs viable local industries and opportunities for its people to learn new skills. The means to conduct affairs of state begin in these seemingly modest concerns.
after: A small country's independence rests on the ordinary family's rice bowl. Only when farmers can pay their taxes, labourers can find work and merchants can carry goods to a buyer can the government afford its officials, schools and soldiers. If those who produce are crushed under rent, debt and idleness, every great affair of state can only be squeezed out of them.\n\nForeign capital brings money and know-how, and the overlord is willing to carry part of the load. But to be heard among these powers, the country's industries must run on their own, and its people must learn new skills.

before: Government expenditure rests on the work of people who must first earn their own living. Farmers need buyers for their harvests, artisans and labourers need employment, and goods need roads and ports to reach their customers. A lasting obstruction at any point spreads hardship to others.\n\nOur existing industries provide a place to begin. When these businesses can employ people and earn an income, households will have something to put aside, and the country will have the means to consider a more distant future.
after: The treasury's money comes from what the people produce, and the producers must first feed themselves. Farmers must sell their harvest, artisans and labourers need work, and goods must get over the roads and onto the ships before they reach a buyer. Let any link stay blocked for long, and poverty passes all the way down the chain.\n\nWe start with the industries we already have. Once the workshops can hire people and turn a profit, households can put something by, and only then can the country speak of the future.

before: As industries begin to earn an income, the provinces need more people capable of managing public affairs. Tax collection, local services and the education of children cannot depend indefinitely on favours among a handful of acquaintances. Teachers and administrators need dependable salaries, while those pursuing an education need some prospect of employment when it is complete.\n\nEstablishing these institutions will give the government a lasting claim on local support. At least some of the taxes people surrender should return to them as public services on which they can depend.
after: Now that industry earns an income, the provinces are short of people who can get things done. Collecting taxes, running public business and teaching children cannot depend for ever on favours from a few acquaintances. Teachers and clerks need salaries paid on time, and students need to see where their learning will take them.\n\nAt least part of the taxes people hand over ought to come back to them as schools and public offices they can use.

before: Centres of population and wealth need the produce of other regions, whose farms, mines, fisheries, forests and workshops in turn need wider markets. However plentiful a region's resources, they will bring little income to its inhabitants while producers remain cut off from buyers.\n\nThe government must encourage production in both regions and open the routes along which their goods can travel. A common market allows different products to complement one another, and places with related industries to divide their work. If these businesses prosper, both regions will have reason to maintain their ties.
after: The crowded, wealthy places need the produce of other regions, and the farms, mines, fisheries, forests and workshops of those regions need bigger markets. While producers and buyers stay apart, no amount of wealth in the ground will put money in the inhabitants' pockets.\n\nProduction must be built up in both regions, and the road between them opened. Regions with different produce can trade what each lacks; those with similar trades can divide the work. Keep the business going long enough, and neither region can do without the other.

before: Goods already pass between the regions, but the people who administer public affairs cannot all remain in one place. Taxes come from both regions, and administration and education need a footing in both. Otherwise, every increase in production will leave more local affairs to be decided far away.\n\nThe government needs people to undertake this work and schools to train their successors. Giving local inhabitants the skills to enter new occupations will spare the country from having to seek every capable official in the same few cities.
after: Goods already move between the two regions, but the people who run public affairs cannot all crowd into one place. Taxes are raised in both, so offices and schools must take root in both. Otherwise, the more the provinces produce, the more of their business must be referred to someone far away.\n\nThe country needs people to do the work, and schools to train those who will follow them. When local people can take on new posts, the country need no longer search the same few cities for every capable hand.

before: Independence or extensive autonomy allows us to decide more of our own affairs. It also places a greater share of the burden of trade and defence on our government. People expect freedom from interference to bring some improvement in their lives.\n\nIndustries need materials and customers, the provinces need schools and administrators, and the army needs support. The wealth and abilities of our people must sustain these institutions if our political freedom is to endure.
after: Independence, or broad autonomy, means deciding many things for ourselves, and carrying the burden of trade and defence on our own shoulders. The people want to be free of outside meddling; even more, they want their lives to get better.\n\nThe workshops need materials and buyers, the provinces need schools and officials, and the army must be paid. Only if the country's own resources can bear all this will self-rule be more than a phrase.

before: Hardship is encouraging local people to seek a common remedy. Some demand changes to the ownership of land and the conditions of labour. Others want a greater voice in public affairs. Burdens once borne by each household alone are becoming the demands of a movement.\n\nThe government may allow them to organise, promise a response through legislation, or send the police to silence them. Those who enjoy the existing arrangements and those who seek to change them will judge from our response whose interests the government intends to defend.
after: When life becomes unbearable, people in the provinces band together to find a way out. Some want new rules for land and hired labour; others want a say in national affairs. Hardships once suffered behind each family's closed door have become the demands of a movement.\n\nPermit them to organise, promise legislation, or call in the police: whatever the government does, landlords, employers and those who want change will all see whose side it is on.

before: Local administration and industry need literate, skilled people. Fund a year of public provision to help residents qualify for new occupations.
after: Offices and workshops alike lack people who can read and have a trade. Spend a year of public funds teaching residents new occupations.

before: Merchants and guilds hope to expand within the present market. Support their use of established trading routes to find more buyers for local production.
after: Merchants and guilds want to grow their business within the market we already belong to. Follow the existing trade routes and find more buyers for local goods.

before: Prepare a market of our own, taking responsibility for the supply of materials, production and the sale of our goods.
after: Open a market of our own, and keep materials, production and sales in our own hands.

before: Use our present autonomy to develop our laws, market, public services and defence.
after: Now that we govern ourselves, our laws, market, public business and defence are ours alone to run.

before: Point to the strength of our local economy and administration, and ask the overlord to let us manage more of our own affairs.
after: We can collect our own taxes and staff our own offices. It is time the overlord handed more of our affairs back to us.

before: Propose peaceful independence to the overlord, seeking a negotiated end to subjection and responsibility for our own domestic and foreign affairs.
after: Negotiate with the overlord and end our subordination with dignity, taking full charge of our own affairs at home and abroad.

before: Ask the present market owner to let us establish our own market, taking responsibility for supply, demand and transport.
after: Ask the owner of our market to let us set up on our own, running supply, demand and transport ourselves.

before: Our existing industries are beginning to provide farmers and labourers with a steadier livelihood. Goods can reach the market, employers can pay wages, and more households can support themselves through their work.\n\nTheir greater security also gives the government a dependable source of taxation. Every sum entering the treasury was once part of a household's living. Peace in the provinces and stability at home require the people who create this wealth to be able to carry on their work.
after: Our industries have begun to give farmers and labourers a steady way to make a living. Goods find buyers, employers can pay wages, and more and more households live by their own work.\n\nWith these households settled, the treasury has a tax base it can count on.

before: Administration and education now have foundations the country can sustain. Public affairs have people to attend to them, knowledge has a means of spreading, and local industries can hope to find workers trained for new occupations.\n\nThe more people learn, the more readily they can take part in national life and explain what they expect of their government. These institutions give the state more capable hands, while requiring those in power to attend more closely to the livelihoods of the governed.
after: The offices and schools are open at last, and they can be kept open. Public business has people to handle it, books have teachers, and the workshops are starting to find hands who can read and know a trade.\n\nThe more people read, the more clearly they can say what they want from their government.

before: Our market relations have changed, bringing an end to the temporary arrangements under which merchants and enterprises operated in the former market. The supplies, customers and transport connections on which they relied must be secured under new circumstances.\n\nA government may change its direction, but producers must still find buyers for their goods. Their ability to carry on trading will shape employment and income in the provinces.
after: We have changed markets, and the temporary deals that merchants and companies struck under the old one have lapsed. Materials, customers and transport must all be found again in the new market.\n\nThe government can change course in a moment; the producers' goods are still sitting in their warehouses.

before: Years have passed without the government bringing law, trade and local enterprise together to sustain its intended programme of self-government. Existing industries and schools can continue their work, but the conditions needed to support the country's affairs remain incomplete.\n\nThe undertaking must be deferred. It may be resumed when the necessary conditions are in place. Meanwhile, the wealth and skills already acquired will need to be sustained through the daily life of the country.
after: Years have gone by, and law, trade and local industry have still not managed to carry our programme of self-government. The workshops and schools we built go on working, but the conditions the state needs have never all come together.\n\nThe undertaking must be set aside for now. When the conditions are met, it can be taken up again.

before: Local industries can now support education and administration, and the country has the market connections and defensive strength needed to sustain its autonomy. With trained people and revenue at its disposal, the government has more to rely on in its dealings with foreign powers.\n\nThe public has paid for these achievements through taxes and labour. What people hope to receive in return is a country in which they can earn their living in peace.
after: Local industry can pay for schools and offices, and our markets and defences are enough to stand on our own. With people and money in hand, the government has more to bargain with when it deals with foreign powers.\n\nThese savings were built up by the people, tax by tax and day's work by day's work.

before: The government has enacted the legal reform it promised to the provinces. Those who organised to demand it now have reason to believe that they can influence national affairs. Practices they once had to endure can at last be challenged in the name of the law.\n\nThe beneficiaries of the old arrangements will hardly forget their loss. Political disputes will follow the new law into everyday life, and the government must ensure that its legislation is enforced.
after: The government has carried out the legal reform it promised the provinces. Those who organised for it now know they can move national policy. What they once had to swallow, they can now challenge in the name of the law.\n\nThe masters who lost by it will not let the matter rest. The new law is on the books; now someone has to enforce it.

before: Hardship among local farmers and labourers is drawing support to the land reform movement. Ownership of the soil and control over labour determine how much they can keep after a year's work, and whether they can escape their old dependencies.\n\nThose who demand change have organised. To answer their demands, the government must challenge established rights and those who hold them. If we merely ask them to endure, what reason have they to place their trust in the present order?
after: Farmers and labourers in the provinces are struggling, and the land reform movement is gaining support. Who owns the land and who commands the labour decide how much they keep after a year's toil, and whether they can ever be free of their old masters.\n\nThose who want change have organised. If we tell them to keep enduring, why should they go on believing in this order?

before: Growing hardship among labourers has brought local support to the labour movement. Workers want a voice in wages, hours and protection at work, hoping to avoid facing their employers alone. Employers see demands that will alter their costs and their authority over labour.\n\nThe government must decide how to treat these organisations. Allowing workers to speak, promising legislation or sending in the police will shape the means by which both sides can defend their interests.
after: Labourers' lives are growing harder, and the labour movement has won hearts in the provinces. Workers want to bargain over pay, hours and safety at work, and no longer face their employers one by one. To the employers, these demands strike at their profits and at their command over their workers.

before: Local liberal and radical movements are seeking wider support. People excluded by their status or political qualifications want a voice in the affairs that govern their lives. Those who already hold power may have little desire to admit them.\n\nThe advocates of wider participation have organised, and the government can no longer leave the argument on paper. Whether it permits their activities and is prepared to change the law will determine how these people regard the state.
after: Local liberal and radical movements are rallying support. Those shut out by birth or political qualification want a say in the affairs that rule their lives; those already inside are in no hurry to make room for them.\n\nThey have organised, and the argument can no longer be kept on paper.

before: The government of [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] points to progress in its economy and administration as grounds for managing more of its own affairs. It argues that it can now bear these responsibilities, and that the overlord's restrictions should be relaxed accordingly.\n\nAcceptance will grant the local government greater autonomy. We must judge whether less interference will preserve this relationship, and how much we are prepared to spend to retain our present authority.
after: The government of [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] cites the progress of its economy and administration as grounds for running more of its own affairs. By its account, it can bear these responsibilities, and the overlord's restrictions ought to be loosened.\n\nIf we agree, its autonomy will rise one step.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] seeks a negotiated end to subjection, with its own government assuming responsibility for domestic and foreign affairs. It hopes that recognition of independence will allow the two countries to live at peace.\n\nAgreement means relinquishing our overlordship and the disputes its maintenance might provoke. Their demand reaches beyond freedom to administer a few matters locally: they wish to decide the future of their country.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] asks to negotiate an end to its subordination, with its own government taking charge of affairs at home and abroad, and the two countries remaining at peace after independence.\n\nWhat they want this time is to decide their country's future for themselves. To agree is to give up our overlordship, and with it the quarrels we might fight to keep it.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] has asked to establish a separate market and manage its own production and trade. Its merchants and producers would have to arrange their supplies and find their buyers, changing the existing exchange of goods between our countries.\n\nWe must decide whether to grant this freedom.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] asks to set up a separate market and run its own production and trade. Its merchants would arrange their own materials and buyers, and the existing flow of goods between our countries would change with it.

before: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] seeks a defensive treaty with our country. It hopes to gain an ally on whom it can depend, while we would gain a partner in resisting attacks from abroad.\n\nOnce a treaty is signed, an attack on our partner may bring us into war. This friendly proposal asks something of our army and treasury as well.
after: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] asks for a defensive treaty with our country. They want an ally they can count on.\n\nOnce the treaty is signed, an attack on them may draw our army into war.

before: The government is preparing to propose a common defence agreement to [SCOPE.sCountry('small_receiver').GetName]. Relations are friendly and our territories lie close together. Armies able to support one another would give a foreign aggressor reason to hesitate.\n\nThe envoys have drawn up their proposal and await our decision.
after: The government means to propose a common defence to [SCOPE.sCountry('small_receiver').GetName]. Our countries are on good terms and our borders lie close; if our armies can support each other, an aggressor will have to think twice.\n\nThe envoy's letter is already drafted.

before: Whose realm is Southern Ming: the Zhu emperor’s, or the Zheng family’s creation? Nanjing retains the imperial succession, while the Southern Administration in Hangzhou commands the troops and revenues that sustain reform. The Western provinces and Hangzhou could postpone their dispute over sovereign and minister while resisting the North. With reform reaching deep into provincial life, they can no longer avoid the question of who will govern.\n\nHuguang’s academies and Xiangfan’s troops uphold the Zhu succession, while Sichuan’s republicans continue to debate the Southern Administration’s reforms. Governors in the Southern Seas and lords in Japan weigh the land, money and soldiers a new dynasty might demand. Representatives in the Assembly of Rites, ministers in the cabinet and provincial commanders will eventually have to answer for their choices.
after: Whose realm is the South: the Zhu emperor's, or the one the Zheng family carved out? Nanjing still holds the Ming succession; the Southern Administration in Hangzhou commands the troops and revenue that drive reform. While the Western provinces and Hangzhou stood together against the North, the question of sovereign and minister could wait. Now reform has reached deep into the provinces, and neither side can dodge the question of who governs.\n\nHuguang's academies and the Xiangfan garrisons keep the Zhu calendar; Sichuan's republicans are still arguing over Hangzhou's reforms. The governors of the Southern Seas and the lords of Japan are reckoning up how much land, money and manpower a change of dynasty will demand of them.

before: The Ming court and Hangzhou press rival claims. Remain outside the succession dispute for now and attend to our own trade and defence.
after: Let the Ming court and Hangzhou quarrel as they please. We will look after our own trade and defence.

before: As the court disputes the succession, seek control of our own taxation, appointments and defence. Make our position clear to both Ming and Wu.
after: While the court fights over the succession, take our taxes, appointments and defence back into our own hands. Make that plain to Ming and Wu alike.

before: The accompanying ministers have reached the court’s refuge, and the local government is making room for them. Its army must still raise supplies and its administrative commissions govern the province; now it must also maintain the travelling court. Ming loyalism has acquired a centre to serve, and the host must bear the first costs of breaking with Hangzhou.\n\nEnvoys continue to arrive from the provinces and overseas states. Claims once debated in the Assembly of Rites and cabinet must now be sustained by military strength.
after: The ministers who followed the sovereign have reached the refuge, and the local officials are busy settling the court in. The garrison here must still raise supplies and draft men, the administrative commission must still govern the counties, and now there is a travelling court to feed as well. Ming loyalists finally have a sovereign to serve; and the host province has become the first to break openly with Hangzhou.\n\nEnvoys from the provinces and overseas states are still on the road. The claims once argued in the Assembly of Rites and the cabinet will be settled by soldiers from now on.

before: Neither Huguang nor Sichuan can presently receive the court, which must remain in Nanjing. Ming loyalists must continue seeking provincial support while negotiating with Hangzhou, which controls the troops and revenues. The Zheng claim to the throne is already before us; deliberations in the capital will determine how much room remains to act.
after: Neither Huguang nor Sichuan has a government able to receive the sovereign, so the court must stay in Nanjing. Ming loyalist ministers are canvassing the provinces with one hand and parrying Hangzhou, which holds the troops and the money, with the other. The Zheng bid for the throne is already on the table.

before: Opponents of the new dynasty have not formed a coalition capable of taking up arms. Appointments, taxation, military obligations and overseas status remain disputed. Hangzhou must keep answering those demands if Zheng rule is to win acceptance, while Ming loyalists continue seeking allies.
after: Those who oppose the new dynasty have not yet formed an alliance able to take up arms. Appointments, taxation, military costs and overseas status are still bitterly disputed. If Hangzhou wants the Zheng title to hold, it must answer each of these claims in turn; meanwhile, Ming loyalists are still searching for men who will stand or fall with them.

before: The provinces have broken with the centre, but circumstances have changed in the government chosen to receive the court. Unable to leave the capital, Ming loyalists must seek another host in Huguang or Sichuan capable of protecting the sovereign and maintaining the court. Every further day in Nanjing makes it harder to escape Hangzhou’s arrangements.
after: The provinces have broken with the centre, but something has gone wrong with the government that was to receive the court. The sovereign cannot leave the capital for now, and loyalist ministers must keep writing to Huguang and Sichuan, looking for someone strong enough to protect him and rich enough to keep a court. Every extra day in Nanjing is another day at Hangzhou's mercy.

before: Appointments, taxation and military funding require a constitution that the Southern realm can uphold. Send our proposed settlement to the provinces and overseas states to seek their support.
after: Appointments, taxation and military funding need a constitution that everyone accepts. Send our proposals to the provinces and overseas states and ask them to declare their support.

before: The previous negotiations failed, and opponents of the new dynasty still command their own territory and troops. Reopen the confrontation and demand an answer concerning the central government’s authority.
after: The last negotiations came to nothing, and those who reject the new dynasty still sit behind their own troops. Confront them again: do they recognise the court or not? Make them give a straight answer.

before: The cabinet’s envoy has arrived in [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] to seek our support for a settlement preserving the Ming dynasty. A constitution will define the powers of the centre and provinces. The Zhu sovereign will remain at the head of government, the cabinet and Six Ministries will administer under law, and provincial delegates will participate through the Assembly of Rites.\n\nAcceptance commits our government to the Zhu succession and this settlement. We retain our government, territory and existing laws. The status and commerce of overseas states will continue to be governed by their separate treaties.
after: The cabinet's envoy has arrived in [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] to seek our support for a settlement preserving the Ming dynasty. A constitution will define the powers of the centre and provinces. The Zhu sovereign will remain at the head of government, the cabinet and Six Ministries will administer under law, and provincial delegates will participate through the Assembly of Rites.\n\nTo agree is to recognise the Zhu succession and back this settlement. Our government, territory and existing laws are left untouched, and our dealings with overseas states, as subjects or as trading partners, remain as our treaties provide.

before: The Southern Administration’s envoy offers clear terms: recognise Zheng accession and place our Chinese territories under direct central administration as provinces. Their separate military and political authority will end; appointments, taxation and military funding will fall under the new dynasty’s constitution and the cabinet and Six Ministries.\n\nThis would complete the centralising reforms long pursued by Hangzhou. Accepting means deciding who will govern and tax these lands. If our country also holds territory overseas, its government and boundaries there will be retained.
after: The Southern Administration's envoy offers clear terms: recognise Zheng accession and place our Chinese territories under direct central administration as provinces. Their separate military and political authority will end; appointments, taxation and military funding will fall under the new dynasty's constitution and the cabinet and Six Ministries.\n\nThe centralising reform Hangzhou has pursued for years lacks only this final step. Once we agree, the question of who governs these lands and who taxes them will be settled for good. Any overseas territory we hold keeps its government and borders.

before: The Southern Administration asks us to recognise the Zheng succession and surrender any territory we hold in Shikoku and Kyushu to direct Wu rule. Our government would retain its remaining lands.\n\nThe proposal ties a Southern dynastic succession to Japan’s borders. Acceptance would secure our place in the new order, at the cost of those territories. The court and the great houses must weigh that price before answering Hangzhou.
after: The Southern Administration asks us to recognise the Zheng succession and surrender any territory we hold in Shikoku and Kyushu to direct Wu rule. Our government would retain its remaining lands.\n\nSo the Southern succession has been tied to Japan's borders. Accepting it buys a place in the new order, and the price is these lands.

before: The Southern Administration asks [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] to recognise the Zheng succession while retaining our government, territory and existing status. The Assembly of Rites and cabinet will settle the Southern constitution’s distribution of sovereign and provincial powers. Our commerce, ports and military obligations will remain matters for separate treaties.\n\nThe Zheng family needs recognition at home and overseas. Before answering, we must consider the place this succession would leave for our country.
after: The Southern Administration asks [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] to recognise the Zheng succession while retaining our government, territory and existing status. The Assembly of Rites and cabinet will settle the Southern constitution's distribution of sovereign and provincial powers. Our commerce, ports and military obligations will remain matters for separate treaties.\n\nWhat the Zheng want is support, at home and abroad.

before: For a year, the provinces and states supporting Ming have upheld their commitment to reform. The provisions debated by provincial delegates in the Assembly of Rites on appointments, land taxes and military funding now have a basis for enactment. The cabinet asks [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetPrimaryRoleTitle] [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName] to proclaim a constitution defining the powers of the centre and provinces.\n\nSince Chen Dongyang restored provincial administrative commissions, the Southern government has coordinated civil and military affairs, but the titles of former feudal lords still sustain local influence. Disputes set aside during resistance to the North can at last be settled in the assembly. The Zhu succession will endure, with sovereign, cabinet and provinces each exercising authority under the constitution.
after: For a year, the provinces and states supporting Ming have upheld their commitment to reform. The provisions debated by provincial delegates in the Assembly of Rites on appointments, land taxes and military funding now have a basis for enactment. The cabinet asks [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetPrimaryRoleTitle] [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName] to proclaim a constitution defining the powers of the centre and provinces.\n\nSince Chen Dongyang restored provincial administrative commissions, the Southern government has coordinated civil and military affairs, but the titles of former feudal lords still sustain local influence. Disputes set aside during resistance to the North can at last be settled in the assembly. The Zhu succession is saved, and from now on the sovereign, the cabinet and the provinces each act under the constitution.

before: [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetPrimaryRoleTitle] [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName] has proclaimed the revised constitution. Provincial delegates participate in the Assembly of Rites; the cabinet and Six Ministries conduct central government; provincial administrative commissions administer local affairs under the settlement. The Zhu house has gained room to govern beyond Hangzhou’s domination, while accepting constitutional limits on the sovereign.\n\nThe settlement preserves Southern Ming’s Confucian form of constitutional democracy and federation. Its provinces and overseas states retain their governments and territories, and the centre assumes the expense of maintaining the new institutions. Powers once contested by the Southern and Western Administrations through military strength now have an agreed constitutional basis.
after: [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetPrimaryRoleTitle] [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName] has proclaimed the revised constitution. Provincial delegates participate in the Assembly of Rites; the cabinet and Six Ministries conduct central government; provincial administrative commissions administer local affairs under the settlement. The Zhu house has won back room to govern from under Hangzhou's thumb, and the price is a throne bound by the constitution.\n\nSouthern Ming survives as a Confucian constitutional democracy and federation. The provinces and overseas states keep their own governments and territories, and the centre pays for the new institutions. The powers that the Southern and Western Administrations once fought over with soldiers now have a constitution both sides accept to decide them.

before: Chen Dongyang’s reforms have carried the Southern provinces beyond the military fiefs of the old Northern Ming order. Yet a deliberation in the assembly cannot by itself dissolve the grievances between the Southern and Western Administrations. With the parties supporting the same settlement, the centre must meet the agreed administrative expenses and put its proposed distribution of powers into practice.\n\nOverseas states also await fulfilment of the court’s commitments. Sustaining these arrangements month by month may bring the succession dispute back within reach of negotiation.
after: Chen Dongyang's reforms long ago turned the Southern provinces into something other than the military fiefs of old Northern Ming. But the bad blood between the Southern and Western Administrations will not melt away after one debate in the assembly. Now that the parties stand behind the same settlement, the centre must produce the administrative funds it promised and turn the constitution's paper powers into practice.\n\nThe overseas states are watching to see whether the court keeps its word. Only by honouring the settlement month after month can the succession dispute be brought back to a point where it can be talked out.

before: Stop the additional administrative expenditure for the settlement, ending this effort to ease the court dispute.
after: Stop the extra administrative spending for the settlement; the effort to calm the court dispute through it ends here.

before: After the succession, the Zhu relatives remaining in [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] still need homes and support. Providing for the former imperial family preserves their status and shows their old followers how the new government treats its predecessors. The people and obligations left by centuries of imperial rule cannot vanish with a change of dynasty.
after: After the change of dynasty, the Zhu relatives remaining in [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] still need food, clothing and a roof. Supporting these princes without a throne lets them keep their dignity, and lets the old dynasty's followers see how the new one treats its predecessors. Centuries of imperial rule do not vanish with a change of name.

before: The succession dispute has lasted two years without a settlement acceptable to all parties. The Southern provinces and overseas states continue to exercise their existing powers, while the divide between Ming and Wu has not produced a common war.\n\nWe can close these constitutional negotiations and accept the present borders, governments and treaty relations. Neither side will have fulfilled its programme of reform, but the realm need no longer wait for a constitution that remains beyond agreement.
after: The succession dispute has dragged on for two years, and the court has still not brought the parties round to a single position. The Southern provinces and overseas states go on governing with the powers they have, and the split between Ming and Wu loyalists has not grown into a common war.\n\nBetter to let it rest here, and accept the borders, governments and treaties as they stand. No one's reforms have been carried, but at least the realm need not keep waiting for a constitution no one can agree on.

before: Continue the negotiations.
after: Keep talking.

before: Wu and the remaining belligerents are still in confrontation. Each surviving holdout must decide its own course once it leaves the fighting.
after: Wu and the Jingnan states are still facing each other. Any state that drops out of the fighting must find its own way forward.

before: Envoys from [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_holdout_sender').GetName] seek our protection. Their government offers to accept our suzerainty in return for preserving its territory and army. Accepting would give us a new responsibility in the southern dispute.
after: Envoys from [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_holdout_sender').GetName] seek northern protection. They will acknowledge the empire as overlord if only they may keep their land and their army. Take them on as subjects, and the empire has set foot in the Southern war.

before: We will not undertake this obligation.
after: The South's mess is not the empire's to clean up.

before: Northern protection has not materialised. The envoys’ journey has left us with the same choice: defend our country against Wu again, or end the struggle by submitting.
after: The North will not lift a finger. The envoys made the journey for nothing, and the same two roads lie before us: fight Wu again to keep our land, or, if we will not fight, submit.

before: The envoys have returned with acceptance. Our territory and army remain intact, and the northern empire is now our overlord. Restoring livelihoods and order after the war remains our task.
after: The envoys have come back with the North's acceptance. Our land and army are safe, and the North is our overlord now. Life after the war is still ours to rebuild.

before: Provide assistance to poor and marginalized communities, encouraging their participation in a shared social life. Those who enjoy established privileges may resent the expense.
after: Pay subsidies to the poor and the discriminated against, so they will want to join in a common social life. Those who hold the old privileges will only see money taken from their own plates.

before: Give politically marginalized communities greater attention in national affairs. This unsettles the government’s established base of support while creating room for a shared national identity.
after: Give those long pushed to the margins of politics a voice in national affairs. The old foundations of power will be shaken, but a common national identity will have somewhere to take root.

before: Dongzhou has long been established along the Pacific coast, and its support helped establish the Mexican republic. American expansionists envision the western ports, pastures and trade routes as part of the Union. Extending the republic from the Atlantic to the Pacific will require the federal government to secure these territories and bear the cost of confronting the western states.
after: Dongzhou has long been established along the Pacific coast, and its support helped establish the Mexican republic. American expansionists still draw the western harbours, pastures and trade routes into the Union's future. If the republic is to stretch from the Atlantic to the Pacific, these lands must belong to the Union, however many talks and however many wars it takes with the western states.

before: Indigenous peoples and Mongol pastoralists travel the routes across the Great Plains, while Dongzhou's soldiers and merchants press farther inland. American settlers, land speculators and frontier officers want these territories brought into the Union. Community lands, pastoral routes and national borders are at the centre of another struggle for the continent.
after: Indigenous peoples and Mongol pastoralists travel the routes across the Great Plains, while Dongzhou's soldiers and merchants press farther inland. American settlers, land speculators and frontier officers all want these lands drawn into the Union.
